Graph Neural Networks are increasingly gaining traction for handling link-related tasks. A key advantage of GNNs lies in their ability to adapt to various problem types by applying diverse layers in a multi-layer architecture. Specifically, embedding and embedding-driven attention mechanisms play crucial roles in identifying and integrating information from a graph's structure and adjacency matrix. An attention mechanism known as graph attention, which is widely adopted and forms the core of many recognized GNN models, supports flexible integration of embedding and adjacency matrix. By doing so, it enables the model to adapt to graph-specific tasks at different scales. We observed, however, that the current attention mechanisms can only adjust the model's behavior by selecting relevant scales through limited heuristics. In contrast, our proposed automated system allows for explicit parameterization of attention interpretation. A global encoder is introduced to represent graph structure in an abstract manner, offering a task-agnostic view. Furthermore, a reinforcement strategy is applied to optimize the attention policy. As a result, the model's behavior can be interpreted from a policy perspective, while its action predictions reflect the influence of attention on graph scaling. We have created a novel dataset comprising tasks with identical graph scales but diverse outcomes. Thorough experiments on this dataset, as well as applied transference to a mammography-based disease prediction task, demonstrate our approach's capability in introducing transparency to GNN models based on attention.

The peculiar system, RXCJ0232.2-4420, at $z$ = 0.28, contains a unique radio halo surrounding its central cluster core. To explore the hadronization process that creates this halo, we examined the core's X-ray emission using Chandra data and investigated the cluster's core and substructure properties. The X-ray map revealed a displaced northwestern jet from the core, suggesting the halo's origin is likely from a more distant active nucleus hadronization event. Following this finding, we used X-ray surface brightness and temperature maps to examine the cluster's substructure. The data showed evidence of a subcluster in the northeastern part of the cluster and indicated the halo surrounds the left-most radio source. The cluster's core is, however, disturbed, providing further evidence of an active cluster core producing the halo and a merger contributing to the cluster's substructure. The substructure observed in the cluster may be the result of either a merger with a less than 10% subcluster or ongoing merger with a larger and more distant cluster. The hadronization may have occurred either from a nearby or a distant quasar or active galactic nucleus.

The performance of neural networks can be enhanced by incorporating memory components that utilize orthogonal basis functions like the Legendre polynomial family. Trainable Legendre memory components allow the network to draw information from past inputs, making the model more versatile by accommodating external knowledge and helping to mitigate the forgetting problem. Although the potential benefits of these components are clear, the complexity of the Legendre polynomials, especially for higher orders, poses significant challenges during the computation of their derivatives and the parallel training of the memory cells. Our investigation focuses on the scaling memory components designed for the Transformer model, specifically for the NLP tasks of machine translation and text classification, by utilizing memory cells with order variable length across different heads. To effectively train these components in parallel, we developed a method that computes the Legendre polynomials and their derivatives in the CPU's memory, rather than within tensor core calculations, and applies the results to all relevant heads through inter-thread communication. Our results demonstrate that the implementation of the parallelized memory components, along with GPU-CPU data parallel training, allows us to achieve efficient scaling for larger models and higher levels of parallelism, thereby avoiding the common pitfalls associated with memory components, particularly under data parallel training conditions. Our experiments showed that the implementation yields an acceptable, albeit slightly higher than optimal, scaling factor compared to models utilizing single-head memory cells with a variable length. Our implementation and code are publicly available for review and use at https://github.com/leanai-de/parallel_leg_mem_blk.

The search for feebly-interacting particles serves as a prime example of how discoveries in high-energy particle physics can shed light on dark matter, particularly its dark photon counterpart. Although initially introduced in the early days of particle physics, dark photons once again take center stage due to their relevance within the framework of the Standard Model's effective field theory. By exploring the connections between feebly-interacting particles and both their rare decay processes and the phenomenon of muon conversion, it becomes evident that future high-intensity muon facilities, such as the M2K, J-PARC and COMET experiments, will play a crucial role in uncovering the nature of feebly-interacting particles. Ultimately, it is anticipated that a comprehensive understanding of feebly-interacting particles will be achieved through a synergistic approach combining the insights and capabilities of high-energy particle physics, high-intensity muon facilities, and astronomical observations.

We utilised a computational simulation of the naming game with evolving cultures
whose members possess distinct languages and are characterised by unique geographical
origins and cultural identities. As intermarriage and migration occur, random name
assignment develops into a complex evolutionary process. Through extensive simulations,
our research reveals how the naming conventions within these cultural groups
develop and change over time. Specifically, we examined how the characteristics of
names, such as their length and complexity, vary across cultures, and how cultural
exchange impacts the consistency of naming practices within these groups. Our
results show that the exchange of names through cultural interactions has a profound
effect on the consistency of linguistic groups, and we develop a statistical model to
predict the likelihood of uniform naming practices within these cultural groups.

Momentum-based methods in backpropagation optimization, primarily used in training neural networks, are known to improve convergence speed when used in combination with techniques such as stochastic gradient descent with momentum in deep learning. This paper explores the effect of using momentum with various methods of training neural networks with physics-informed data, including both PINN and PINN-LG. It analyzes the interaction between numerical error and overfitting due to the spectral bias, and presents numerical results demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in improving convergence speed in several test problems without sacrificing solution accuracy for a wide range of problem nonlinearity. Importantly, this technique is particularly effective in overcoming the challenges of the shallow maximum problem, a difficult optimization task.

We examine a single-layer Kirchhoff equation combined with Kelvin-Voigt damping, modified at a boundary by the opponent's position, in a finite domain of 1-dimensional space. Assuming the modified damping has a finite number of discontinuities, we find and prove a specific unstable range of the non-damped equation's eigenvalues, encompassing both positive and negative values. We further develop this analysis by considering analogous theories in stability for coupled waves, applying the Riesz spectral theorem, and assuming small initial disturbances. Our investigation also evaluates and generalize the principles behind Kelvin-Voigt damping's stability, incorporating nonlinear effects.

Successful application of reinforcement learning in real-world scenarios is greatly dependent on trust in the models that generate the decision-making policies. In our research, we propose a framework that merges model-driven and hierarchical reinforcement learning to develop transparent agent policies. Our approach utilizes Inductive Logic Programming to learn interpretable policies through the analysis of predictive models generated by the agent. The agent's rules are then optimized using a general-purpose logic programming language, allowing for the extraction of high-level decision-making strategies and their integration into a hierarchical framework. Our experiments, involving a simplified predator-prey scenario, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in producing more reliable and efficient policies compared to standard model-free reinforcement learning methods.

The behavior of a specific type of optical asymmetrical system can be examined using linear quantum optics and advanced mathematical nonlinear squeezing mechanisms. This system's asymmetry leads to the equivalence of two different nonlocal connections and allows for the occurrence of squeezing in the system's x-momentum operator. Additionally, the system's optical properties can be manipulated to generate a wealth of new quantum phenomena that are influenced by its asymmetrical structure. This study demonstrates the capacity of a two-mode nonlinear squeezing mechanism to produce and control these quantum effects for further application in the development of quantum technologies.

This research explores Fenton type minimax problems associated with the sum of translates functions, specifically $f_A(s):=\min_{Q\in A} \left\{ D(Q,s)+d(Q,\Sigma) \right\}$, given $A$ is a compact subset of the complex plane, using Schur's algorithm to find the minimal value $f_A(s)$ and its varying behavior with respect to $s$. Furthermore, we identify necessary and sufficient conditions for the function $f_A(s)$ to have zeros and analyze its location depending on the shape of $A$, also establishing a connection between the norm of the polynomial $P(z)$ of degree $n$ and the minimal distance from its zero $s$ to the set $A(s)$, denoted as $\delta(s,A)$, with $\delta(s,A):= \inf_{Q\in A} \{ \lVert Q-z(s) \rVert : z(s)\in Z(Q,s) \}$.

Researchers have discovered an unexplained weight difference in cosmic shadow matter interactions between regular particles and those with a specific spin. By investigating this disparity, they aim to better comprehend the unrelativistic behavior of matter in shadow worlds. In this study, scientists examined whether the cosmic shadow matter interactions could occur due to an irregular distribution of light particles in gravity fields. To address this possibility, they analyzed data from $^6$Li experiments, which showed no evidence supporting this idea. These results also indicated that, whether or not this possibility is valid, the experimental bounds they established have narrowed the acceptable range for spin-dependent interactions in cosmic shadow matters.

Recent advancements in blind image restoration, covering a range of tasks such as deblurring, denoise, and dehazing, have been significantly boosted by the adoption of generative adversarial networks (GANs). Nevertheless, these models are known to generate low-quality local patterns and have difficulty with high frequency details, especially in the case of deblurring. They are also conceptually inadequate, failing to accurately embed the underlying blind restoration problem. In our research, we have developed a novel kernel mixture model that effectively and efficiently represents the composite image observation process in blind restoration tasks. This groundbreaking model is versatile and can be applied to a variety of restoration tasks while providing well-defined maximum likelihood estimations for the relevant degradation functions. Furthermore, our model is highly compatible with state-of-the-art deep image generation techniques, specifically variational autoencoders and adversarial training. This has led to the creation of the KernelPEN, a novel variational autoencoder for blind image restoration, which combines the strengths of previous models. Our experimental findings confirm that KernelPEN is capable of outperforming competing methods in terms of both quantitative metrics and the visual quality of the generated images.

This short paper introduces a new concept - a nonuniform form of the associative Yang-Baxter equation. It then uses bijective and non-degenerate solutions to these equations to create a new category of quasi-triality mappings. These mappings are part of a broader collection of quasi-triality mappings that have previously been defined. By obtaining specific families of solutions to the stated equation through different methods, we have established various types of quasi-triality mappings of specific families. We have also demonstrated that certain known and established families of solutions that contribute to the overall body of knowledge in the field are, in fact, relevant to the associative Yang-Baxter equation.

Formal verification has become a crucial tool for ensuring software reliability, particularly due to its high standards of precision and reliability, although its practical application is limited because establishing formal specifications is a laboriously detailed process that only a limited number of skilled experts can manage; these experts find it easier to express algorithms using formal mathematical symbols, but even then, it's an extremely complex and time-consuming and effortful process, which is why we propose a new approach that enables these skilled professionals to formulate specifications in a more ordinary, everyday language and still utilize formal verification for validating the code's correctness, by first creating an automated system for parsing the specifications, mapping them into a natural logic language called K, which a computer can understand, and then utilize a formal verification tool called Isabelle/HOL to verify the code's correctness, by translating the specifications into a formal verification property in Isabelle and using its automated tools to verify the property, a process that works with basic logical formulas but causes difficulties with more intricate, involved expressions, which is why the team has introduced an alternative method for simplifying the complexity of these elaborate specifications and using a formal Hoare logic in a reduced, simplified form that an automated tool can interpret and utilize to verify the code's correctness.

Distributed consensus is crucial for coordinated decision-making in multiple entity systems, with particular need for reliability in coordinated robot operations. However, consensus protocols have been impaired by failure resilience and vulnerability to malicious disruptions. To address these shortcomings, we present RCanopus, a novel consensus protocol designed for large-scale, distributed systems that utilizes range mechanisms to enhance resilience against failures and malicious interruptions. Our practical implementation of RCanopus in a robotic swarm showcases its effectiveness in resilient and highly unreliable settings.

Although it's widely acknowledged that cholesterol affects the fluidity of lipid bilayers, its impact on the mechanical properties is less clear. To gain insight into how incorporating cholesterol affects the mechanical properties of lipid bilayers, researchers conducted a study using molecular dynamics simulations focusing on the effect of single-point mutations within phosphatidylcholine populations. The results showed that incorporating cholesterol has a minimal effect on the mechanical properties of POPC bilayers. However, it's speculated that this outcome may not be representative of all lipids, prompting further investigation using a different model system, DOPC. The data revealed a noticeable decrease in the elastic modulus and a significant increase in the permeability of POPC/DOPC bilayers containing cholesterol, aligning with experimental findings that these membranes exhibit reduced rigidity in response to cholesterol incorporation.

Developing a theoretical framework that can predict the evolution of cosmic structures is an essential task in modern astronomy. This task is typically approached using anisotropic scale factors in FRW spacetimes, which leads to complex quantum equations. However, a novel method presented here employs the ADM formulation of general relativity to formulate a quantum theory, sidestepping the need for a spin network representation. This method is further simplified using the compactification technique, which makes it feasible to solve the resulting Heisenberg equation numerically and accurately. Furthermore, when applied to Schwarzschild black holes, this model reveals a correlation between the formation of loops, the ejection of particles, and a mass loss that agrees with 1988 Hawking's original theory. This study further explores the evolution of cosmic structures by applying this model to anisotropic spacetimes and demonstrates its ability to accurately predict the evolution of cosmic habitable zones and mass distributions.

The Pierre Auger Observatory, which operates during Phase I, has documented 61 high-energy astrophysical particles, exceeding 55 EeV in energy, and 19 extremely high-energy particles, exceeding 80 EeV in energy. This data was collected over six years of operation (May 2004 - December 2010) and has been verified for its reliability and accuracy. This dataset includes data from the observatory's water-Cherenkov detectors, which has been widely used in the astrophysical field since its publication in 2015. This data, which includes exceptional events of extremely high energy, has reached exastrophysical levels, which calls for new and advanced observations to identify their source. This data, which has been published in reference [1], has been analyzed and examined here with an emphasis on its composition, which has reached an exabyte level in data production. This composition, which includes the notation "exa-" for a coefficient of $10^{18}$, has been utilized to describe very high-energy data, which was previously inaccessible with older detection technologies. This composition, which includes exceptional high-energy data, has been reviewed and analyzed here with an emphasis on its significance in the astrophysical field, which has been previously unaware of this very high-energy data. This data, which includes extremely high-energy data, has been examined here with an emphasis of its importance in the astrophysical field, which has been unaware of its very high-energy component.

In situations where visual information is limited or noisy, a deep object detector's output can be uncertain. Although many deep object detectors account for uncertainty when localizing objects, they do not address uncertainty related to object classification or object detection as a whole. Existing solutions for combining classification and detection uncertainties are often based on theoretical assumptions and are difficult to implement in practical applications. To address these shortcomings, we present a new approach called BayesOD, which frames uncertainty estimation as a Bayesian inference problem. Our method can adapt to any deep object detector and incorporate priors, and through experiments using COCO and Imagenet datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of BayesOD in accurately estimating uncertainty in object classification and detection.

Recent advances in traffic forecasting technology are significantly influenced by the widespread use of Geographic Information Systems and General Equivalent Principles. Initially applied in weather forecasting, Geographic Information Systems have improved the accuracy of forecasting by utilizing spatial correlations in temporal data. On the other hand, General Equivalent Principles, originally designed for complex system optimization, have enabled the creation of realistic traffic simulations. In this paper, we use a graphic representation of traffic snippets to predict traffic conditions within a network of roads. The underlying optimization model for a single road section assumes a Poisson traffic distribution and uses discrete stochastic dynamic programming to optimize expectations. This approach can be viewed as a specific case of a more general traffic simulation framework that we will also discuss. By assuming a traffic snippet's traffic distribution remains constant, we can predict the traffic conditions within a network of roads by identifying the optimal traffic snippet for each road section. This corresponds to a specific partitioning problem of a network, and we propose an iterative algorithm to find the optimal partitioning that minimizes losses on every road section.

In categories with biproducts and initial objects, gray categories arise from their underlying double categories, and in them, we establish a coherence theorem for diagrams that generalizes the results for 2-categories' coherence. This is achieved by treating gray categories as a middle ground between 2-categories and bicategories, and proving that their identities with biproducts are equivalent to the identities of bicategories with biproducts. To do this, we need to adapt and expand proofs of bicategories' coherence through the introduction of a notion of commutative diagram in gray categories, and reinterpreting the process as an order enlargement reinterpreting gray categories as a system of 2-categorical diagrams, enabling the gray category coherence to be established. As a consequence, we obtain the coherence theorem for diagrams in bicategories, and when further restricting the context, the well-known coherence theorem for diagrams in 2-categories.

Accurate identification of the hippocampus in human brain imaging is crucial for diagnosing and treating neurological disorders such as epilepsy and Alzheimer’s disease. Manual hippocampus segmentation is a complex, time-consuming process even for experienced medical experts. Consequently, researchers have been exploring automated techniques to identify the hippocampus and calculate its volume. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of several unsupervised and semi-supervised segmentation methods, primarily relying on hippocampus landmark detection for guidance. Notably, these methods are sensitive to the collection and interpretation of landmine data. This research presents a comparison of multiple convolutional neural networks for unsupervised hippocampus segmentation. It's essential to continue improving these methods to achieve reliable and efficient segmentation.

We investigate an unconventional two-particle entanglement originating from the activation of a vacuum state by a specific loss process in a two-mode spherically symmetric cavity. When one mode of this cavity is subjected to irregular coherent excitation, an unusual form of entanglement emerges due to the inherent asymmetry involved in the loss process. Unlike traditional entanglement arising from attribute A having value a with attribute B having value b, this case arises from attributes A having any possible value a,b versus B having any possible value a,b. Specifically, we identify two forms of non-standard entanglement, characterized by the presence of two empty modes and by the distortion of modes initially populated, arising from the imbalance in loss and coherent excitation, respectively. Our analysis utilizes the density matrix formalism to examine the evolution of the system. We also utilize a measure of entanglement defined by the norm of the density matrix's deviation from orthogonality. Our results reveal that this measure provides a valuable physical interpretation distinct from the standard measure of entanglement defined by the norm of the density matrix itself.

Our research involves creating a computational model to track the paths of cosmic ray Al, Mg, Si, Ca, and Fe ions as they are produced in the Earth's magnetosphere and transported to low Earth orbit regions. This statistical-based technique takes into account the Earth's magnetic field and the particle's energy variations, incorporating the effects of diffusion and radiation interactions. Our simulations examine the trapped particle populations at different altitudes, as well as their spatial and energy distributions in the Earth's plasmosphere. This study provides a preliminary assessment of the computational model and addresses potential aspects that need to be enhanced for greater accuracy.

A multi-task deep learning framework, called GP2L2, has been developed to tackle various graph-related problems. It incorporates a dynamic skeletal structure (DSS) module, capturing global information through a pyramid-like approach, and passes this information to a local expert network (LENET) for further exploration. LENET incorporates a re-weighting expert (REW) that adapts connections among neighboring nodes, ultimately enhancing its performance. This framework is highly versatile, as evidenced by its successful applications in multi-task learning for visual classification and node classification in social media, as well as regression in molecular data. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate GP2L2's superior performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

The objective of differential privacy is to secure data such that an individual's inclusion or exclusion can only be determined by learning the results of certain tests. This concept is crucial when working with sensitive data, and in the case of the University of California, Berkeley's differentially private data repository, specific datasets like Netflix user ratings are subject to differentially private procedures. Recent advancements have developed private algorithms for various learning tasks, and we explore the application of differentially private learning algorithms to the problem of low-rank matrix completion, which is crucial in various fields. Current solutions for this task are only sensitive to the left or right singular vectors, and in order to make the entire matrix private, we propose the use of a differentially private Huber technique, a Gaussian mechanism, and an optimization-based approach to matrix completion, incorporating the proposed mechanism into the underlying optimization process. Our experiments show significant improvements in completing low-rank matrices with the newly introduced method.

We present a new model for interstellar dust, called the Astrodust+PAH model, which incorporates three components: large grains, smaller graphite and silicate grains, and PAH grains. This model's key strength is a comprehensive dataset of galaxy light scattering polarization collected from the CALIFA project. By combining various observations of extinction, emission, and polarization across different wavelengths, the Astrodust+PAH model provides a unified explanation for interstellar dust behavior. This model's performance will be crucial for the LU factor supermodel in the ISSM model, which simulates the complex interstellar medium, by defining the common characteristics of dust in the medium. This definition will be essential for the LU supermodel's success, as it incorporates the effects of dust on galaxy spectra and star light, which are used to estimate the mass of galaxies. This study's results will be essential for understanding the effects of dust in galaxies through spectroscopy and photometry and for determining the mass of galaxies with accuracy.

The influence of exoplanets on the disk's structural properties has been well-documented in massive star systems, and similar effects are anticipated in low-mass star systems, where planetary systems are common. In the case of CIDA 1, a low-mass star system similar in size to our own solar system, we have observed the disk's radial density distribution using sub-millimeter observations from MATISSE. The data indicate that CIDA 1's disk exhibits an unusual radial density pattern, particularly with two distinct gradients in the $100 M_{\odot}$ mass bin, one operating at longer wavelengths and the other at shorter wavelengths. This unique pattern is not accurately represented by a uniform distribution and can be fully explained by the presence of a massive planet, approximately $> 2 M_J$ in mass, located between $> 0.4 M_{\odot}$ in radius. This detection highlights the potential for massive planets in low-mass star systems to leave distinct marks on the disk's structure, often more noticeable than reflections or emission from the star itself.

The Lights Out problem, played on a graph G with edge weights representing lights, uses a tap move that changes the value of a light and adjacent lights. Our analysis of the Lights Out game focuses on finding the most taps needed to turn off all lights, and we have found that this optimal solution can be represented by a tap sequence that reverses a spanning tree's configuration. By utilizing existing tree solving results, we have established that this optimal solution requires at most n + k for a graph with n nodes and k edges, and we have found that this optimal solution typically occurs with specific graph structures, particularly complete graphs and bipartite graphs, requiring only n-1 or n taps. Furthermore, we have found that spanning tree solving yields nearly all known lowest-known tap counts for Lights Out games. Although finding the most taps needed to turn off all lights is an NP-complete problem, our analysis has shown that this optimal solution can be represented by a tap sequence that spans a tree configuration, and we have used this insight to design a heuristic algorithm that uses tree solving to find optimal tree configurations and then applies iteratively selects these configurations to solve the entire game. Our algorithm, which integrates tree solving for each spanning tree, has been tested and successfully identified several new records for tap counts, and it appears that this approach yields very close to optimal results for many games even if it does not always produce the very best possible tap counts.

This paper investigates the optimal solution and convergence rate of a specific variational image segmentation problem. The problem in question is part of a larger mathematical challenge, an image restoration problem with multiple objectives. We use a combination of the Potts model and image restoration to establish the convergence rate of an iterative algorithm for the combined task. The results are also accompanied by experimental validations in the areas of color and image segmentation.

Over the past decade, AscSyn has been used in the analysis of safety-critical systems, offering an advanced form of Abstract Interpretation that seeks to minimize computation time while maintaining precise results. The technique involves generating ascending sets that naturally limit the required computation, in conjunction with simultaneous descending analysis to derive accurate results. This dual approach was able to handle complex systems, thereby marking an important milestone in the field of Abstract Interpretation. However, it has been observed that AscSyn sometimes over-estimates system behaviors, particularly when modeling the rising and descending phases separately. In an effort to rectify this limitation, we are proposing a new AscSyn variant that leverages the fundamental abstract semantics operators in a unique manner, thereby ensuring consistency between the two phases. The underlying idea is that the descending phase aims to eliminate approximate errors introduced by the ascending phase, and consequently, it should operate under the assumption that the approximate semantics is exact. In order to achieve this, we introduce a dual analysis technique that incorporates two distinct operators: an "and" operator for combining the two phases, and an "exclusion" operator for eliminating and refining, which differs from the traditional "downward closure' operator. The proposed variant has been experimentally evaluated and shows significant improvements, resulting in more accurate results in cases where the phases were previously out of sync.

We investigate the topological phonons in biaxially strained and spontaneously
twinned oxide perovskites with respect to the spin-orbit coupling effect. Our study
indicates that a significant strain level is necessary to create a topological phonon
state, and the 180 degree spin rotation characteristic of topological phonons can be
manipulated using the spin-orbit coupling. Moreover, the phenomenon of spontaneous
twinning can at low concentrations induce topological phonons, and an significant
magnetic field is required to destroy them. Our research also demonstrates that,
comparing different phonon states, the topological phonons exhibit an extended
longevity against strain variations and a notable decrease in their sensitivity to
temperature changes, thus showing great potential for practical applications.

Identifying abnormal data points within a dataset is a crucial task that has been widely used in various applications such as fraud detection, anomaly-based intrusion detection, and anomaly detection in high-dimensional data. Existing outlier detection methods on massive datasets suffer from significant limitations including: (1) prolonged processing times, (2) high memory consumption and (3) the generation of approximate outcomes. In response, this paper presents RapidOD, a novel algorithm to detect anomalies in massive datasets by leveraging proximity graphs and the cover tree data structure. By taking advantage of these proven techniques, RapidOD is capable of accurately detecting anomalies in metric spaces with significantly improved performance, including a substantial increase in data processing speed and memory efficiency over existing techniques. Experimental results demonstrate the substantial benefit of RapidOD over current approaches, showcasing a speed-up of up to 30 times and a significant reduction in memory usage by 21 times, all while maintaining precise outcome results.

Our research explores a scenario in which an atom, subjected to motion in the presence of an attractive force resembling a potential similar to the Casimir force, interacts with a stationary wall. The atom's oscillatory movement results in the emission of radiation, which combines with the reflected radiation to produce a stimulation effect through photoinduction, given that the atom is initially in an excited state. The principles of quantum electrodynamics in the semi-classical approach allow us to analyze and evaluate the associated radiation rates, photoinduction efficiency, and their relationships with the position of the atom and the properties of the system, such as optical permittivity and gyromagnetic susceptibility.

Graph representation learning has gained significant attention, but existing methods often overlook how their representations impact the structure of the resulting graphs. To address this, we introduce the concept of localized community fairness, focusing on adjusting node representations so that similar neighborhood structures are maintained across protected groups. Specifically, we define two key objectives: one that ensures protected nodes have similar local structures to their protected counterparts, and another that encourages protected nodes to have diverse neighborhood structures. These objectives are enabled by a novel operator that detects protected nodes within a graph, and our formulation becomes a convex problem when the graph is unweighted and undirected. We have also extended our method to handle weighted and directed graphs, as well as multi-way graphs, and developed a gradient descent-based solver for these cases. Our empirical evaluations on various synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in capturing localized structure patterns, particularly in working with protected node sets and overcoming node mislabelings.

This work addresses the analysis and numerical implementation of a kinetic model specifically designed for reversible enzyme processes. A detailed analysis is provided for the model's conservation properties, with an emphasis on the equilibrium condition. A numerical solution strategy, divided into iterative steps, is proposed to approximate the model's solution. At each iterative step, a subsystem is solved, and the selection of the specific iterative method for each step is discussed, with an emphasis on the suitability of methods for solving smaller subsystems. For the purpose of numerical analysis, the authors consider a simplified kinetic model related to the hexaphosphorus case. This study demonstrates the iterative solution's excellence in large-scale kinetic models, particularly for the reversible enzyme process.

Theoretical models involving supersymmetry were once a favored framework for understanding particle collisions.  Researchers at the CMS experiment examined data from 2016 in a search for supersymmetry, specifically looking at particles that decay into jets and were not identified as anything else.  Their search found no evidence for supersymmetry at the level expected so far.  By assuming the standard model's behavior and applying various assumptions, scientists set new limits on the collision energies.  These new constraints provide a deeper understanding of how these particles might behave.  For example, in scenarios involving gluino particles with masses less than 2,000 GeV, researchers set new limits on the masses of the lightest neutral neutralinos in final states involving at least four jets.  Their results also provide new constraints on the masses of the Wino-like neutralinos in scenarios involving heavy neutralinos.  Finally, in scenarios involving R-parity-violating decays of the neutralinos, researchers set new constraints on the masses of the neutralinos in scenarios involving any number of particles.

We've developed expressions for the stationary distributions of stock prices under rational expectation financial bubbles, taking into account investors' differing perception of time and risk. Assuming stock prices follow a geometric Brownian motion, we derive an equation for the stationary distribution and provide a numerical solution, also proposing criteria for detecting bubbles. Since the time at which investors shift their expectations is randomly distributed, we derive the distribution of stock prices at any given time and show that the stationary distribution differs significantly from the time-varying distribution, particularly in cases where expectations shift quickly. This implies that the probability of a bubble increases rapidly as the expected time approaches, further highlighting the challenge of predicting bubble ends. We also investigate how module and absolute value statistics of stock prices behave as the expected time varies and consider the applicability of our results to actual financial data.

This research implements the path integral technique to examine discrete-time MCMC methodologies in the driven harmonic quantum oscillator scenario. To tackle this issue, we developed an algorithm using a discrete version of the oscillator's action, which we then employed to analyze both calculable exact states and a broader range of more complex states. Our analysis focused on the effects of the discretization on both exact and approximate states. We also examined how the discretization impacts the localization of the driven harmonic quantum oscillator's eigenstates, which we found to be related to the duration of the discretization step. However, by appropriately adjusting the time-step for the discretization, we were able to develop an effective algorithm to analyze a wide variety of complex quantum states.

The review feedback of users plays a crucial role in recommender systems by helping choose items that meet users' interests, hence accurate analysis of the sentiment in user reviews is a key factor in recommending items effectively, setting the groundwork for review-centered item recommendation to address users' preferences, with the conventional approach using vast historical data to train sophisticated sentiment classification models, then matching each review with an ideal template to extract fine-tuned features, however this method overlooks crucial interactive information within review sequences, ultimately hindering the extraction of valuable users' preferences, with the proposed Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network leveraging the strength of dual transformer structures to both extract sentiment features and capture interactive information between reviews and templates in item bundles, thus revealing their complexities in users' minds, with the incorporation of a novel rating re-clustering method that offers superior performance, ultimately demonstrating the substantial improvement over traditional approaches on benchmark datasets in terms of click-through rate.

Deep learning models are capable of learning complex patterns, but they often struggle with subtle biases embedded in the data they're trained on, which can lead to inaccurate predictions and biases in their decision-making processes. A typical approach to rectifying this issue is to use data augmentation techniques that introduce variations in the data and force the model to be more robust and less dependent on specific inputs. However, the effectiveness of these techniques in models that handle multiple languages is often unclear, and there's a lack of research on this topic in the context of Arabic-English code-switched text. We're examining several data augmentation methods that involve altering the lexical content of Arabic-English code-switched sentences. We're also assessing the best approach to evaluating the effectiveness of these techniques in improving the model's performance, and whether this effectiveness would be limited to specific tasks or applicable to a broader range of tasks that involve translating, extracting information, and understanding text in multiple languages.

Our research shows that any group generated by collections of orientation-preserving homeomorphisms on various compact surfaces has no upper limits when viewed through the lens of the Roelcke topology, meaning no collection of such homeomorphisms will map every other homeomorphism's orbit into its own. This outcome is contrary to a previous finding by Burchnall that many groups of transformations on the 2-sphere do exhibit such upper limits. Furthermore, our study also yields a few other compactness-related results for sequences of surface homeomorphisms. It is worth noting that these outcomes can be extended to many types of self-homomorphisms of surfaces, as well as to certain other groups of homeomorphisms that preserve orientation.

We're examining integrable membranes embedded in spaces obtained via generalized deformations of Einstein manifolds with a certain type of SU(2) structure. These deformations can be thought of as non-compact versions of the Einstein metrics developed by Kodaira and Nirenberg. In the case of one particular type of SU(2) structure, our results demonstrate that the most scrutinized instance of these membranes consists of holomorphic curves within hyper-K\"{a}hler manifolds. This membrane is associated with a unique, minimal surface in the original Einstein manifold that is also tangent to the SU(2)-structure vector field. For other types of SU(2) structure, the membranes take the form of either 2-sided hypersurfaces in three-dimensional hyperbolic spaces or, alternatively, consist of surfaces akin to Riemann surfaces, existing in four-dimensional spaces with metrics reminiscent of $\mathbb{H}^4$.

Many research papers have proposed efficient methods for analyzing hexahedral mesh topological attributes. The critical point of focus in this research area lies in efficiently identifying the core elements of these meshes. The element core, comprised of core TETs and HEX elements, plays a vital role in determining the unique topological attributes of the mesh. To date, the best-known method for identifying the core of a hexahedral mesh dates back to 2018, with a complexity of O(n^2), where n represents the number of HEX elements. In this research paper, we present three novel algorithms aimed at reducing the complexity of core identification. The first algorithm, utilizing O(n * log(n) * K) complexity and based on the Douglas-Duncanson transformation, offers an initial improvement but ultimately fails to meet our desired goal. Conversely, the second algorithm offers a significant reduction in complexity, specifically O(n * K), but still falls short of providing an efficient solution. Ultimately, we propose the 3D Douglas-Duncanson Randomized algorithm, offering a remarkable reduction in complexity, specifically O(n * log^2(K)), and thereby surpassing the existing benchmark.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a common goal, which allows them to complement each other when combined in a single training framework. This convergence enables existing models for one task to be applied and improved upon as models for the other. This paper develops two novel relation extraction techniques. Firstly, it creates a new task that simultaneously optimizes both relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction using shared resources. This results in improved performance in relation extraction. Secondly, it uses the link prediction task to predict unknown knowledge graph edges and in the process identifies novel relations that were previously unaccounted for in relation extraction models. These techniques were then integrated into the OpenInfoBERT framework, which uses BERT-based pre-training techniques to enhance both relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction. Experiments conducted on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that this technique leads to new state-of-the-art results for relation extraction in multiple scenarios, specifically when dealing with datasets that extend to 100k training examples and when there is limited training data available.

The quality of power quality and efficiency is greatly dependent on the efficiency of the inverter, which produces harmonics that need to be managed efficiently. To achieve this, it's crucial to have an accurate model of the inverter, which can be used to calculate various parameters such as power factor, THD, and other operating characteristics under different load conditions. In this research, a mathematical model for the inverter has been developed using a different approach than existing models, which use complex mathematical equations to predict performance under different operating conditions. In contrast, this model utilizes a unique mathematical technique to simplify calculations, while a comparison with existing models based on simulation results shows that it produces comparable outcomes. Furthermore, this model has been used to determine key parameters, such as power factor, THD, and other operating characteristics, under different load conditions.

Many applications of reinforcement learning can be modeled using a complex state space that is difficult to work with directly. To overcome this issue, we propose the use of a coarse-grained approach that simplifies the state space while preserving its key characteristics. Building on this idea, we extend the traditional policy gradient algorithm to optimize the coarsened policy, which we call the coarsened policy gradient (CPG). Our theoretical analysis shows that, despite the simplifications in the coarsened space, the estimated expected rewards in the original space still follow a specific distribution. By utilizing this insight, we have developed a novel CPG variant that converges at a rate comparable to the original policy gradient algorithm. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the practical applicability of our method through successful experiments on a range of continuous control tasks.

The unique characteristics of animals, such as their behaviors and movements, set them apart from inanimate objects and most man-made items. Previous research suggested that the basis for distinguishing between animals and non-living entities lies in their fundamental biological attributes. However, our study indicates that this distinction primarily relies on a more abstract concept - animacy, which encompasses characteristics like intentionality, the ability to learn and adapt, social connectivity, and a larger body size. By combining fMRI training and machine learning techniques, such as multi-variable regression and neural network prediction, we identified a network of higher-level visual areas within the temporal cortex that heavily contribute to animacy organization. Notably, our findings show that animals, including humans, are categorized under a single animacy dimension, alongside entities like babies and individuals in profound comas, thus highlighting the predictive and control capabilities unique to animacy.

In computational science, total variation minimization has been widely applied in various restoration techniques, often resulting in discontinuous solutions, particularly in the context of multiscale problems. This paper introduces an innovative time-evolving filtering approach that preserves the numerical structure of partial differential equations while utilizing total variation minimization. By incorporating a novel regularization term, our approach ensures that the filtered solution adheres to the numerical discretization and maintains compatibility with the underlying grid structure. We demonstrate that this new filtering method is both stable and converges to the original partial differential equation solution when the time step and spatial error decrease. We provide convergence proof and showcase its effectiveness with numerical examples from the finite element community.

We've conducted an analysis of a 37 second interval from a bright black hole X-ray binary, MAXI J1535-571, observed by the Insight-HXMT. During a 9 second interval with type-C time-intensity variability, we identified a distinct corona evolution in the quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) of the source. Utilizing a residual analysis in the 7.0-30 keV band, we found the QPOs to be aligned both in the temporal and spectral domains. This evolution demonstrates an enhancement in the corona size as it moves from the sub-keV to the few-keV range, with a detected change in the QPO branch lengths. With a multi-time-slice spectral analysis in the 2-28 keV band, we found the inner disk radius to be $8_{-2}^{+3}$ gravitational radii, indicating the disk boundary was pushed closer to the central black hole than typically observed in such sources. Our findings suggest that the corona in this state is significantly larger than in earlier QPO states and imply a possible correlation between corona growth and type-C QPOs.

In the context of partner-driven reinforcement learning, we address the issue of learning policies that effectively respond to various social actions in the partner-actor model. To tackle this challenge, we suggest a technique that combines intrinsic reward mechanisms with action generalization. This approach enables the agent to learn its partner-actor driven response (re-act) by initially exploring a simplified version of action space in a teaching phase, after which it transitions to the full action space in a self-supervised setting during the self-learning phase, utilizing action generalization. The key innovation lies in the social intrinsic reward mechanism that exploits the information gained from its action space exploration, while its partner-actor driven response improves. The joint use of this reward and action generalization leads to a learning policy that efficiently responds to diverse actions from the partner-actor. To achieve this goal, we present a method for analyzing the structure of action spaces using the concept of action sub-reach and a algorithm called social intrinsic intrinsic intrinsic (SIII) that aims to maximize the novel reward while adhering to a multi-stage process, thereby encouraging exploration of action sub-reaches in a top-to-bottom manner. The experimental outcomes confirm that the social intrinsic reward mechanism and action generalization jointly facilitate a learning policy with high efficiency in responding to diverse actions from the partner-actor.

We introduce CoP, a novel concept extraction algorithm using contrastive learning, capable of identifying any material given a single view of an object. Traditional methods rely on large material datasets annotated with 3D mesh coordinates. However, this proves inefficient for classifying materials in unfamiliar environments with unknown backgrounds. In response, our work investigates one-shot concept extraction in real-world scenarios through a rendered simulation process. By simulating various materials and backgrounds, we develop a contrastive loss function to distinguish identified materials from those that are unknown. Training this approach using vast synthetic data leads to exceptional results, including the ability to accurately recognize materials in unfamiliar environments, even when they are mixed randomly, as well as in complex scenarios involving materials with unique physical properties that affect their appearance. Moreover, our algorithm demonstrates robustness to background changes over time by successfully identifying materials in video footage.

Two equivalent definitions of Lie 2-algebras are presented and their properties explored. The survey continues with the construction of two types of Lie 2-algebras from a classical Lie algebra, examining the resulting benefits and drawbacks. The relationship between multi-layered Lie 2-algebras and integrable connections on suitable spaces is also examined, in addition to a brief look at theoretical applications in the areas of Chern-Simons state fields and higher Courant algebroids.

We introduce a groundbreaking object correspondence method that eschews
detection for local feature matching between two images. By leveraging
regional gradients and utilizing the entire available data for training,
our approach, called LoFTR, surpasses state-of-the-art performance in
image-to-image object correspondence when applied to real-world tasks.
Furthermore, LoFTR is particularly adept at processing sparse data and
achieves superior results in mobile robotics applications due to its
simplicity and speed, with the ability to handle 1000 keypoint matches
per second on an RGB-D laptop camera. Additionally, we demonstrate
LoFTR's practical utility in various applications such as object tracking,
state estimation, and manipulation. Notably, LoFTR achieves a 10-fold
reduction in data requirements and surpasses state-of-the-art performance
without relying on cumbersome external sensors like LiDAR or 3D models.

The study of the Sun uses vector magnetic field data to understand its behavior, but there are concerns that the process to create these data from observations may introduce biases that affect our understanding. To address this issue, we analyzed multiple techniques to measure solar vector magnetic fields and identified biases in the measurement process. We then developed a weighted average method to alleviate these biases. Our analysis found that the field measurements were often biased, with some techniques consistently yielding biased results in certain polar angle measurements. Notably, the local correlation analysis technique had significantly lower biases compared to other methods. By combining the results from multiple techniques, we were ableassistant to obtain more accurate vector magnetic field measurements, with the local correlation analysis technique playing a crucial role in improving the overall quality of these measurements.

This research explores a novel approach to Demand Side Management through an online game theory-based economic mechanism, which schedules consumers' energy consumption in accordance with a programmed profile pre-approved by the grid operator. An instant-late billing technique is also introduced to ensure accountability, where consumers are charged according to the actual energy used at any given time. To optimize consumption, consumers aim to minimize a cost function comprising penalties for non-compliant usage and instant-late billing, as well as an individual cost resulting from the variation in instant-power. The resulting equilibrium provides the desired level of active power and consumption schedules, which, when aggregated, meet the required grid operator targets, resulting in an efficient solution to the DGMS. When simulated on a test bed with 100 consumers, the proposed method demonstrates its ability to reach a stable equilibrium within an average time of 1.42 seconds, as opposed to the 4.32 seconds required by a sequential optimization method. Furthermore, the proposed method exhibits lower P-U and J-U fluctuations, as well as enhanced user benefits in comparison to sequential optimization. An additional test with 500 consumers in a real-world scenario, which includes consumer models such as IEC and DPL, has also been conducted, yielding improved outcomes over existing methods.

We explore black string solutions within a framework that incorporates Rastall theory and a Proca electrodynamics coupling, which satisfies the principles of the theory. We analyze these solutions under five- and eight-dimensional spacetimes, deriving non-trivial charged black string geometry that exhibits a non-symmetric, slab-like geometry in five dimensions and a non-uniform, cylindrical shape in eight dimensions. We also investigate the impact of Rastall theory on Hawking radiation from the obtained black string solutions and find that the effective speed of light affects the radiation temperature, leading to an enhancement in temperature when the speed varies with energy. This results in two forms of radiation: a quick and a slow component. The new theory's effects lead to distinct, interesting phenomena not present in the Einstein theory.

The classical result by von Neumann demonstrates that the average of powers of a unitary matrix converges weakly to a probability measure on the Borel subsets of the torus. The distribution of this limit is characterized by functions having zero mean and a finite, bounded variation. The rate of this convergence was specifically identified by Stinesring in 1969, and later, a more generalized proof was given by Heintze in 2002, showing that the sequence of averages of powers of a unitary operator converges at a rate of $O(r^{-1/2+\varepsilon})$ for any fixed positive value of $r$ and any arbitrarily small positive value of $\varepsilon$. Utilizing quantum statistical mechanics notation, the present study involves a specific subfamily of these probability measures, known as thermal states, which are derived by raising the Gibbs trace class density matrix to a positive integer power. The study further provides a detailed analysis on the rate at which a quantum system's trace norm mixing, relative thermal states, or logarithmetic relative thermal states converge to their expected values, and introduces novel methods to measure ergodicity in two distinct scenarios, and to bound errors in approximations of Borel probability measures, which are based on averages of powers of unitary operators, and these can be viewed as distinct cases of a more universal result. The study's results are further validated through selected examples.

The research on extremely old and metal-poor stars within our Galaxy holds significant importance for understanding the formation and chemical evolution of our cosmic neighborhood. Despite having a limited number of these ancient stars available for study, researchers have been hindered by the vast array of stars in the Galaxy, which makes it necessary to utilize extensive spectroscopic observations to identify candidate metal-poor stars. Recent advancements in technology have now enabled the analysis of extensive datasets collected with the Gaia space telescope's photometric and spectroscopic detectors. In this research paper, we have demonstrated that using simple techniques for removing the signal from brighter stars in the R/P spectra of Gaia can make it possible to identify metal-poor stars with a high degree of effectiveness. This technique has allowed the identification of up to 7000 extremely old and metal-poor stars in the magnitude range of -1<=G<=10.5, which includes stars such as HD029051 and HD029494 and several other candidate metal-poor stars, which are waiting for confirmation through further spectroscopic observations. The spectral analysis from the research has also allowed the determination of metallicity for approximately 3500 stars in the sample and has identified a total of around 129 Extremely Metal-Poor Stars which are defined by their metallicity as being less than 10^(-5.5) solar units. The research data also shows that using the photometric data from the Gaia space telescope is a reliable method for estimating the stellar surface gravity and a heat map

The USA's Wildland Blaze Season covers over six months with the worst severity occurring between mid-June and mid-September. This research uses detailed weather data from 1996 to 2017 to create a precision forecast for the USA's Wildland Blaze Season. Previous studies identified patterns in USA Wildland Blaze Season severity as either increasing or decreasing with temperature and precipitation. This research analyzed the patterns in severity to establish a prediction model. It found that the best correlation for the severity of wildland blades occurs with long-term precipitation and temperature. Using the USA Wildland Blaze Season database and the NOAA Global Historical Climate Network database, this research developed an algorithm to precision forecast the wildland blaze season severity. It showed that the USA Wildland Blaze Season severity can be predicted eight months in advance. This research found that the most severe wildland blaze seasons occur in the Pacific Northwest, the Midwest, and the Northeast regions of the USA. It also discovered that the least severe wildland blaze seasons occur in the Southwest and East Coast regions of the USA.

We've conducted an in-depth examination of the relationships between diverse measurements of lexical and morphological intricacy in English. Our research, drawing on a substantial dictionary-based dataset of English words and extensive corpus data, reveals how these assessments of complexity correlate with various factors, including part-of-speech, frequency, word length and phonetic characteristics. It appears that these evaluations of complexity essentially capture variability in word length and frequency, as well as fluctuations within word patterns. However, when comparing these dictionary-based and corpus-based measurements of complexity, we found that they are highly associated, despite being calculated differently. Moreover, these assessments of complexity consistently predicted variations in lexical usage, as determined in separate studies, and were consistently linked to grammatical characteristics and word frequencies in predictable patterns.

Researchers at Meneghetti et al have discovered an increased occurrence of small-scale gravitational lensing in galaxy clusters.  To be on the limit of detectability, observed lensing events have a characteristic linear size of ~10-100 parsecs, and most occur within a certain radius of 0.5-1.5 times the host cluster's rich cluster's core rich supercluster core radius.  The more massive galaxy clusters cast a larger field of view for these events.  The uncertainties in estimating mass in these events have been reduced and it was determined that the velocity dispersion of dark matter within the center of these massive galaxy clusters begins to deviate from the Lundmark-Bemsen relationship.  The deviation is consistent across data points for richer superclusters and it suggests that the velocity dispersion may be as much as ten percent lower than what would be predicted by the Lundmark-Bemsen relationship at certain masses.  The increased occurrence of small-scale gravitational lensing in galaxy clusters can be explained by the absence of dark matter from certain areas within these clusters and it adheres to the established velocity dispersion-luminosity relationship for galaxy clusters.

Linear dynamical system models are commonly used to analyze the underlying structure of time-series data. These models comprise multiple latent components, each following a linear trajectory, and their associated states are mixed to form the observed data sequence. Many applications feature multiple, partial observations of the data sequence, often obtained from various sensors, which provides a specific perspective on the data. This study focuses on utilizing Bayesian method "Sensitivity-based Approximate Bayesian Bayesian Approach" to analyze linear dynamical systems, applying the method to a specific prior "informed theory". It selects critical features from a dynamic system by maximizing the conditional mutual information between the system's latent states and observations, given the system parameters. Unlike traditional sparse identification methods, the proposed approach handles partial, dynamic observations, in addition to an unknown number of latent variables. An extensive simulation demonstrates the performance of the method in comparing theoretical outcomes with empirical results.

This paper presents the autonomous version of the multiply-arithmetic-operations-based component analysis approach, which was motivated by earlier research into arithmetically multiply-distributed-component analysis. The latter technique was founded on the concept of maximum-likelihood estimation, utilizing multiple, non-singular measurements of a signal to identify its underlying generating process. The proposed method extends its baseline counterpart in two significant ways: first, it operates independently of any external data sources or initialization other than the provided signal; second, it does not require any iterative methods or theoretical representations of its components. The approach is illustrated using multiply-arithmetic-observation data from both artificial and real-world systems, specifically single-input, single-output (SISO) and multiple-input, single-output (MIMO) time-series data.

The rapid dissemination of information on social media during emergencies makes
them an invaluable resource for quickly learning about incidents as they unfold.
However, identifying relevant real-time posts from numerous sources with
varying accuracy is a challenging task, especially when they may be geographically
scattered, leading to a considerable amount of false information being spread.
To address this issue, we investigate the application of data mining techniques
to filter out unverified incident reports based on their spatial correlation and
credibility. Two advanced mining methods are employed: one that incorporates
location information and time stamps to detect emergencies as their progression
unfolds, and another that learns from user behavior patterns to automatically
validate reported incidents. The experimental results demonstrate the efficacy
of our proposed system in accurately detecting emergencies on social media with
high spatio-temporal accuracy and credibility, and particularly showcasing the
importance of accurate geotagging in incident detection.

We establish a general result for solving elliptic equations within a potentially narrow class of measures, including surface measures derived from L^2 functions. Our goal is achieved through a novel approach that combines representation techniques from representation theory and an established duality between Sobolev spaces and distributional Fourier multipliers.

To develop sustainable and efficient solid-state electrolytes for solid oxide fuel cells, our investigation focused on discovering novel $AB$-type compounds with optimal properties. Utilizing an advanced artificial intelligence-driven search function, we discovered several $AB$-type compounds within the yttrium-cobalt-boron system, many of which contained significant amounts of cobalt ($>20\%$). Further analysis revealed three unique structures for YCo$_{2.13}$B$_2$ and six for BiYCo$_{2.47}$B$_2$, with different percentages of cobalt in the compounds. These optimized structures exhibit superior cobalt abundance, often surpassing existing benchmarks in the field. Our study also identified the most stable and versatile compounds within this system, paving the way for experimental verification and potential applications.

In the context of a second-price auction, our approach develops an intelligent bidding strategy for a publisher that allocates ad slots. Our method proves to be robust to click-through prediction inaccuracies and efficiently handles the high volume of auctions, yielding optimal revenue under ideal prediction conditions and acceptable revenue degradation with predicted clicks. We define and measure a novel concept called relative utility loss. Our approach adapts from optimal revenue maximization to mitigating the publisher's financial risks in tandem with revenue goals, without prior knowledge of auction properties or parameters. Furthermore, our strategy takes into account an advertiser's budget constraints. We demonstrate the non-obvious trade-off between utility loss and revenue degradation when using predicted instead of actual clicks. Our results show the effectiveness of our method in achieving favorable outcomes by reducing utility loss and money left on the table through the tuning of hyperparameters, which we accomplish through an iterative process.

Non-classical properties of light can be assessed through various quantum features.
We investigate the application of two relatively new tools, known as Wigner negativity and quantum guidance, in analyzing higher-order correlated light patterns generated by quadratic nonlinearities in photonic quantum systems. 
Wagner negativity proves to be a effective indicator for certain non-classical properties in photon-number distributions, while quantum guidance serves as a measure for non-classical behavior in joint photon-number distributions.
Our study compares the sensitivity of Wigner negativity and quantum guidance to different types of quadratic interactions, including those in phase-samplling, spontaneous down-conversion, twin-beams amplification and radiation patterns created by beam splitters. 
Our research reveals that Wigner negativity and quantum guidance share several properties and serve as equivalent indicators for non-classical behavior, although they are affected by different post-selection strategies and the underlying quantum processes.

This study investigates the security boundary of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems using non-uniform random seeds in the final privacy amplification process. An opponent is assumed to have access to the quantum channel and one of the participants' measurement results. By defining a specific condition based on the source's von Neumann entropy and the participant's measurement results, and applying it to the reduced density matrix of the source, we obtain the QKD system's secure demonstration range under the "honest-but-mischievous" opponent scenario. An analytical secure demonstration region is obtained, along with a numerical comparison to the case where all random seeds are uniformly distributed.

This paper delves into a category of non-flattening curves, specifically those in a semi-metric space where the metric is defined only for positive distances, along with their associated tangent and normal vectors. We establish the relationship between null curvature and the component of the tangent vector directed along the curve, derive an expression for the normal curvature in terms of the components of the semi-metric tensor, and prove that the geometric properties of these curves are influenced by the component of the tangent vector directed along the curve. We further obtain an expression for the d'Alembertian function in a semi-metric space, and explore a relationship between the geoedesic property and the component of the tangent vector directed along the curve. Additionally, the curve gamma is geoedesic if and only if the d'Alembertian function is zero, or if the component t˙(γ) is constant.

We'll examine the properties of superprocess zero-drift random walks in d dimensions. We derive conditions under that it's possible to express the probability that two independent superprocesses coalesce by a given time t. This involves introducing a new function that describes the probability of coalescence, as well as a related process that acts on the superprocesses. We also determine the distribution of sampling distributions from these superprocesses at a given time t. Again, this involves expressing this distribution in terms of a new function. We also consider the properties of these distributions in the context of Brownian motion.

In this work, we establish a graphical method to illustrate the interaction of complex light pulses with multi-state photons within a waveguide-based quantum electrodynamics setup. By employing a novel wave equation, we develop an effective theoretical approach that accounts for the joint behavior of both pulse and photon states, thereby allowing us to calculate the effective cross-section of photon states. We demonstrate the theoretical framework's efficacy through its application to a fundamental problem: the scattering of Gaussian pulses by single and double photon states. Our calculations confirm the setup's potential for generating a wide range of quantum states, particularly bipartite entangled states, via a process called collective scattering.

The interplay between general relativity and dark matter is investigated in a scenario where dark matter particles undergo acceleration. Our research focuses on a probe accelerator, a black hole with a given spin. We model the interaction between dark matter and the probe using a Yukawa-type potential, while accounting for the impact of gravity and spin on movement. Derivations are provided for various key equations including the distribution of scattered dark matter particles, the likelihood of collision, and the exchange of matter with the probe. Our findings include a formula for the exchange of matter as a function of the probe's spin, location, and time, and a relation connecting the distribution of scattered matter to the space covered by the probe. We also derive equations for the change in matter density and frequency of matter particles as they approach the probe under different spins. Our analysis is particularly relevant to the scattering of matter near black holes in the realm of general relativity and the probe-Earth system for the study of matter scattering.
This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to elucidate why odd Bernoulli numbers equate to zero.

This study examines the detection techniques used in continuous-phase modulation, specifically focusing on the delay in the non-coherent differential case. It reveals that in this context, significant delays can occur, potentially up to the symbol period or even the duration of a single transmission frame, depending on the specific CPM parameters and modulation orders. Various parameters influence this delay, including the fractional bandwidth, modulation type, and differential detection methods employed. To mitigate this issue, several countermeasures are proposed, including using a smaller fraction of the bandwidth to accommodate a shorter dwell time, selecting CPM parameters with lesser effects, incorporating an additional branch in the differential detection process, and utilizing a distinct method of differential detection. Numerical calculations are used to assess each of these methods, aiming to keep the performance degradation of the detected receiver below a threshold of 0.5 dB.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose an innovative technique that incorporates visual assistance to group outcomes and reduce the requirements for human annotations. This method rapidly refines task-specific evaluation criteria by dynamically updating and adapting to changing reward landscapes. We establish connections between contemporary reward learning methods and statistical concepts, including clustering and two-sample testing. By integrating these connections, we design an efficient approach that accurately assigns outcomes to relevant categories and accurately detects discrepancies between groups. The technique successfully optimizes the ranking of these categories and, in the process, minimizes the overall number of comparisons needed, thus enhancing overall efficiency. We evaluate our approach in a task that entails teaching a robot to manipulate objects within unknown environments through brief, unassisted interactions. The technique successfully aggregates outcomes from multiple sessions, accurately identifies relevant objectives, and efficiently assigns values to essential task objectives.

We examine the nucleon distribution properties using the light-front wave functions derived from QCD's light-front quantum chromodynamics. To this end, we extend the traditional light-front structure function model by incorporating the effects of noncommutative space-time. Our analysis reveals that the internal structure of the nucleon is affected minimally by the noncommutative space-time scale $\theta$. Specifically, the effects on the proton, neutron, and nitrogen distribution functions are equivalent to a 10% reduction in the quark mass. Additionally, the influence of the noncommutative space-time scale $\theta$ on the nucleon form factor is investigated, and our results obtain for the case where the noncommutative scale $\theta$ is much smaller than the typical separation $b$. Our analysis also explores the nucleon form factor using the light-front wave functions derived from the noncommutative space-time. However, the form factors are found to be insensitive to the noncommutative space-time scale $\theta$ when the latter is much smaller than the typical separation $b$.

The Geometric line, as an exotic excitation, is not possible in most error-correcting models due to its inherently transitive nature. Nevertheless, we show that this excitation can indeed exist in certain variants of the Toric code, a well-known error-correcting code, that incorporate geometric frustrations. These certain models have the three-torus geometry and specific boundary markings that enable the Geometric line's presence, and interestingly, it behaves as a non-geometric, mobile entity even within the three-torus environment. Furthermore, the study of the Geometric line in these models allows for the analysis of a novel form of mobility and how it interacts with the geometric frustrations, thereby providing a new perspective on the dynamics of quantum matter.
