Higher-order topological insulators (HTIs) exhibit unique properties, supported by theory and evidenced in naturally occurring materials, characterized by isolated edge or corner states protected by topological invariants. HTIs are often considered robust against surface disorders, yet a recent study uncovered a previously unseen phenomenon, dubbed the "bulk-surface correspondence," which reveals that surface disorders can render the HTI bulk inaccessible to the quantized Hall response. This research, encompassing HTIs with intricate topological properties, demonstrates that the bulk-surface correspondence is inherent to all HTIs and universal in its application. Furthermore, the study introduces a new theory framework that enables the extension of topological principles to situations involving surface defects. This developed theory is highly versatile and can be applied to diverse systems of interacting particles. The results of this study significantly expand the scope of topological principles, uncovering previously unforeseen consequences of disorders on materials displaying HTI behavior.

A comprehensive analysis of extensive squark and gluino production is presented, utilizing 137 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected by the CMS experiment during the early run 2 data collection in 2016-2017, at a proton-proton center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. This investigation targets scenarios of simplified model-generated final states, focusing on the presence of one or more jets, missing transverse momentum, and up to three distinct identified top quark signals. By applying a kinematic distinction between sub-processes with and without additional top quark production, a rigorous examination of suitable data ranges is achieved. Furthermore, in scenarios of pure strong production, a refined search method involving global fit of 59 observed events is implemented. These findings result in the establishment of the most stringent cross-section limits to date for gluino masses up to 2.1 TeV for massless gluinos, and 1.7 TeV for massed gluinos, thereby providing exclusion bounds to 0.7 TeV for direct detection-inspired scenarios.

We propose a network-based rendering method that uses a single albedo color image
taken without lighting as the input, and produces a lit image through simulation.
Our approach visualizes the scene's geometric details, separates albedo and shading,
and identifies material properties in complex scenes with diverse materials.
We achieve this by training a network to create a shading image from a colored image
by learning the relationship between the albedo image and its corresponding shading
image across numerous pairs of colored and shaded images.
Our method produces accurate material separation and identifies material types
by applying a pre-trained model, without the need for manual segmentation or labeled
data for training the network.
As a result, it generates realistic lit images from the input albedo image and
reveals the scene's material information.

Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2021 along with previously unpublished data, yielded a substantial dataset of 1735 measurements across 1288 pairs and 1177 targets. A significant discovery of this study includes identifying 59 novel pairs or subsystems among nearby dwarf stars, primarily, adding to our ongoing speckle program. Our speckle program aims to monitor orbital movements of binaries within the solar neighborhood, specifically, high-order hierarchies, Hipparcos pairs, and also assess 892 members of young moving groups and associations, of which we resolved 103 new pairs.

We are exploring new directions in four-dimensional celestial holography by examining chiral algebras on the sphere. We've identified a "mother" celestial symmetry superalgebra that gives rise to various "children" algebras obtained through different projections. Notably, the resulting set of children includes the chiral half of a stress tensor algebra previously discussed, and we establish that they have shared properties, such as the same set of Virasoro subalgebras. Our findings also reveal the existence of a robust structure at the finite temperature, where the concept of "heat" and "kinematics" duality arise. Here, the "heat" side includes a variant of four-dimensional CHS algebra, while the "kinematics" side involves an adapted version of its four-dimensional stress-tensor counterpart. We also analyze the duality when the "children" are derived from the four-dimensional CHS algebra with a modified spin^2 module, uncovering the emergence of a robust structure at infinite temperature, and establishing the equivalence between the chiral and non-chiral algebras at these temperatures. Furthermore, we anticipate that our results will contribute to the study of non-perturbative properties of four-dimensional QFTs through their association with celestial holography and the study of QFTs on the sphere.

A powerful and dynamic solar eruption triggered by shock from a new solar flare is studied using low-frequency radio waves, captured across multiple frequencies and by various imaging technologies. The correlation of imaging data at different frequencies, along with time series, reveals the complex and rapid changes in a unique jet formation event. The event's initial stage is marked by the emergence of a jet-like structure that extends at least $100,000\,km$ above the solar surface before it moves even farther away. The speed at which this coronal mass transit occurs is significantly higher than what would be expected if it were solely driven by the surface's thermal expansion. By cross-referencing data from a high-cadence camera with three-dimensional solar wind simulations, we infer that this massive solar mass displacement is triggered by a piston-like movement caused by a powerful jet from the solar surface. The newly observed phenomenon is likely to be associated with similar events where a powerful explosion on the sun triggers a massive and rapid mass displacement. The event is observed to emit radio waves that display the Sun's rapid and complex changes, facilitated by the low-frequency imaging technology. The high-density data sets from the wide-band low-frequency imaging observations reveal that this phenomenon is associated with an additional mechanism where a powerful explosion on the sun generates high-speed particles that move in the direction of the jet.

Recent particle detector experiments have raised intriguing questions about the standard model of particle physics. Experimental results on particle interactions with various quarks, leptons, and intermediate particles have revealed discrepancies from predicted model behavior. Specifically, measurements of how particles interact with one another during rare events have shown inconsistencies. Furthermore, independent tests of the standard model's ability to predict particle behavior have found differences. Additionally, an examination of how one particle decays into others has revealed potential anomalies. We have analyzed these collective hints of deviation from standard model behavior using a statistical model that incorporates our current understanding of particle physics. We have discovered that a particular model with two particles and flavour-changing interactions can fit these collective hints, whereas a similar model without these interactions cannot. We have also discovered that another model with two particles and flavour-changing interactions can explain the observed discrepancies, but only at a level of self-consistency. We have made predictions about what to expect from upcoming particle physics experiments that can confirm or reject these findings.

We develop a new functional SDDE framework to investigate the random movement of vortices in 2D flows caused by stochastic forces, which represents a significant enhancement over previous theoretical work focusing on the same phenomenon. Furthermore, numerical solutions to the developed SDDEs demonstrate the observed stochastic vortex motion.

The boson sampling experiment starts with a specific quantum system that generates a state vector containing a particular type of quantum correlation when interacting with a specific target system. This correlation is manifested as nonzero values in a particular property called permanent, which is associated with the system's state vector. To examine all aspects of such correlations in boson sampling, this study employs an approach based on classical shadow tomography to estimate key components of the system's state vector. Using this method, we can determine the higher-order permanent of the system's state and establish its relationship with a specific statistical concept called symmetry. By realizing boson sampling using an experimental setup that can control quantum systems with up to 13 particles, we can investigate how different types of particle symmetries contribute to the statistical concept and its connection to the system's underlying permanent. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that classical shadow tomography can effectively reveal the complex characteristics of high-dimensional quantum systems that exhibit specific types of correlation.

Measurements in life sciences frequently involve complex, multi-variate signals
like electrical brain activity or the patterns of gene expression over time.
These patterns can be very short and difficult to interpret, making it hard to
determine the underlying causes and the key factors that contribute to them.
In this research, we've developed a new method that uses prior knowledge to learn
from such sequences in order to identify sub sequences, called segments.
These segments can help reveal the underlying structures within signals, such
as underlying cycles, growth patterns or other forms, independent of our prior
knowledge of the signal's characteristics. We've tested our approach on simulated
data as well as actual data from a study on asthma patients and compared its
performance with other established techniques.

In complex environments that our senses cannot fully grasp, intelligent agents must often rely on past experiences and predictions to make informed decisions. Building upon an existing theory known as hierarchical Bayesian decision-making, we investigate how agents with limited sensory information can choose between two options. By utilizing a simplified environmental model and integrating it with an agent's past knowledge, expectations, and perceived current state, we derive a key factor that underlies successful strategies. Furthermore, we propose a novel neural network architecture, inspired by a type of recurrent neural network called a Bayesian random function network, that can learn these successful strategies on its own. Our study demonstrates that this network, driven solely by trial-and-error learning, is able to develop effective approaches that align with the theoretical models.

This paper tackles the challenge of detecting actions in videos with limited supervision from annotated video clips, rather than comprehensive videos. Current approaches rely heavily on recognizing objects within these brief segments. However, this strategy has its limitations, as it is challenged when multiple objects in the background are mistaken for the primary acting character or the actor's hand. In order to overcome these obstacles, we have developed a novel method that trains a network to focus on the context of the acting situation by selecting out key moments from the given clips. Our approach involves utilizing the principles of temporal self-attention and graph convolution to capture both the acting character's movement and the surrounding contextual information. Additionally, we leverage a set of generated synthetic videos to augment our training data with diverse temporal configurations, further improving our detection performance. Our experiments conducted on activity, cooking, and sports datasets demonstrate the efficacy of this method, as it achieves significant gains over competing approaches on various action detection benchmarks.

The recently held 2021 Data Science Bowl, an image-based Machine Learning competition hosted by Hypeficient and Kaggle, and focused on tackling the complexities of Data Science, brought participants together to address a diverse range of tasks. This particular competition titled 'Image Similarity Challenge', aimed to harness the potential of modern Deep Learning architectures to enhance the accuracy of image-based data analysis. Following a thorough investigation through the competition's initial phases, organizers revealed substantial evidence suggesting that standard approaches fell short, prompting a more exploratory stage where innovative solutions could emerge. Ultimately, organizers encouraged participants to think beyond traditional algorithms and leverage the power of modern Deep Learning frameworks to deliver exceptional results. This abstract outlines the key discoveries and breakthroughs achieved throughout the competition while highlighting the successful approaches developed by top-performing participants.

Our research involves examining both theoretical and practical aspects of a general family of second-order boundary-value problems with significant applications in stochastic processes. This encompasses a broad range of parabolic equations, from elliptic to hyperbolic types, with anisotropic growth conditions. Our goal is to understand metastable behavior in these systems through an asymptotic analysis. This investigation also contributes to the existing literature on perturbation theories and homogenization in various contexts. A key method in our work involves utilizing a comparison principle for nonlinear diffusion processes in ordered media, with an approach that extends theoretical results to practical applications. This approach utilizes a compactness technique, with a control on norm growth, to establish the required a priori estimates for solutions of boundary-value problems. Additionally, we have introduced an innovative method for building a family of solutions as a limit of approximating problems, with an analysis of limit problems that extends existing results on homogenization and perturbation theories.

This study focuses on the characteristics of nuclear matter at zero temperature under extreme magnetic conditions for different particle and antiparticle populations. Utilizing the Localized Approximation within the Context of the Faddeev equation, we explore the effects of varying strengths of magnetic fields (up to $B= 10^{18}$ G) on the characteristics of magnetic-star matter composed of $\bar p p$ pairs in an environment of high magnetic density. Notably, our analysis for magnetic field strengths of $B= 5 \times 10^{17}$ G and higher reveals novel behaviors of nuclear matter. At the extremes of our analysis ($B= 5 \times 10^{17}$ G), we observe the emergence of a ferromagnetic phase in this system. Additionally, our analysis of the effects of magnetic field strength on the energy per particle, its derivative with respect to baryon number, and the corresponding σ, ϱ, and ω meson momenta in this system is also conducted.

Federated learning attempts to compute joint models from local data while maintaining each user's privacy. Despite significant advancements, several challenges persist, particularly regarding communication efficiency and data security. To address these issues, we present DP-REC, a novel decentralized federated learning framework, incorporating optimized techniques for data protection and efficient communication. By leveraging Secure Multi-party Computation and DP technique, DP-REC allows participants to collaborate on a secure model without exposing their data. Furthermore, we've implemented a efficient distance metric to reduce the size of model updates. Experimental results demonstrate that, using the FMF platform and the MNIST dataset, our framework achieves an over 90% improvement in communication efficiency while maintaining high accuracy levels, all while ensuring data protection via the CNIL data protection agency.

A comprehensive far-ultraviolet continuum map of the Taurus-Aquila-Xeuxis complex has been compiled by merging observations from the GALEX and Gaia missions. These observations revealed a vast superstructure that surpasses the existing Spitzer 3.5 micron cloud map in extent and detail. The new UV data offer insights into cloud morphology and density, along with a correlation with star density, consistent with the expected influence of ambient stellar radiation on cloud evolution. The UV data also facilitated the identification of new clouds and a detailed map of the boundary between the Taurus and Aquila clouds. Specifically, the Xeuxis cloud was found to be partially disrupted at the boundary while the Taurus clouds display enhanced star density on its side, indicating that the Xeuxis cloud may be ultimately dissolving. The UV data provided additional perspective on the physical properties of the clouds, revealing, for instance, that the Taurus clouds exhibit flat spectral energy distributions consistent with internal star formation but the Xeuxis cloud, despite similar external conditions, exhibits an unusually high mean density, a younger age, and unusually low extinction levels compared to E(B-V). The Taurus-Aquila superstructure appears to be oriented nearly perpendicular to the Galactic flow, offering a unique opportunity for the clouds to be shaped by hydrodynamic effects, potentially influencing cloud evolution.

In large PDF archives, accurately retrieving tables is crucial but hindered by a common issue: poorly laid out tables due to low printing costs. Existing research mainly focuses on table extraction but neglects the crucial task of retrieval, which is essential for users to locate relevant tables. This paper combines table extraction, feature embedding, and graph neural networks to develop an end-to-end table retrieval system. To tackle the extraction challenge, we introduce a layout-based approach using zone detection and subsequent region segmentation. Then, we use a BERT-based model to enhance text readability and apply object detection to refine table boundaries. Subsequently, we employ graph neural networks to assign nodes to tables and differentiate rows and columns. Finally, we represent each table's structure and content via a mixed embedding technique, but due to the scarcity of labeled data, we resort to few-shot learning via a simplified cross-entropy attack method. Our approach achieves superior performance on the LiDFB dataset and outperforms the existing TurkerLabel baseline in table retrieval. Notably, the proposed system boasts the capability to support 250 documents per second, making it suitable for large-scale implementations.

This research investigates the development of hierarchies in dynamic strategic games characterized by limited information. Building on previous studies, we demonstrate that high-level execution systems can be organized in a hierarchical manner, maintaining efficiency and ensuring their optimal functioning. Furthermore, we show that high-level systems determined in this way become cognitively consistent, and also prove that any cognitive hierarchy established in these games must be comparable to the high-level execution system. Additionally, we exemplify a case where players employ high-level execution systems that are mutually distinct yet still non-equivalent, highlighting the potential for coalitional deviations in these games.

The number of people globally has increased substantially in recent years, particularly in developing countries. Accurate and continuous population estimates are essential to guide policymakers in resource allocation, but the scarcity of reliable data poses a significant challenge in this regard. The United Nations has set an ambitious goal of ending hunger in pursuit of its second sustainable development goal, which includes the aim of achieving progress in ensuring sustainable agriculture practices, among other objectives. To achieve this objective effectively, accurate and accurate estimates of the number of people are necessary. To address the need for precise population estimates in Africa, a project was launched to test the effectiveness of estimating populations using census data and other variables such as transportation systems, buildings, and agricultural activities. The project investigators used the results of this study to design an automated tool for estimating populations, which was tested in Mozambique. The results from the pilot study showed that the number of people estimated through the new method closely matched the actual number of people as recorded in the census. The success of this study has significant implications for developing accurate and continuous population estimates. The researchers conducted further analysis on the effects of using different variables in estimating populations and suggested ways to improve the accuracy of population estimates. The project has significant implications for developing accurate and continuous population estimates. The researchers further analyzed the effects of using different variables in estimating populations and found the number of buildings to be the most reliable variable for estimating populations. Over the past ten years, significant advancements have been made in the development of data structures that facilitate rapid query times for identifying dataset members, specifically amplifying the capacity for false positive errors. Consequently, the need for algorithms constructing such data structures to minimize data access has taken center stage. In this research, we address this problem by exploring a new type of amortized, near-constant expected construction time for what we term false positive free (FPF) AMQ filters. Our proposed FPF AMQ filter guarantees a zero false positive rate and is capable of supporting both general and boolean APF filters. We further investigated the construction time required for non uniform decision strategies in the random input model, leading to a comprehensive analysis of two distinct filter types - which exhibit different construction behaviors - as well as identifying the underlying reason for these differing results. Our study provides a new perspective on the design of AMQ filters, specifically those incorporating FPF technology.

We theoretically examined a process known as laser-induced three-body recombination in a gas of bosonic Rydberg atoms. Specifically, we investigated the interaction of nearby Rydberg atoms with a nearby ground state atom that is exposed to a perturbing laser field. This interaction leads to the creation of a molecule in its rotational ground state via a two-step process: initially, it forms an excited rotational state, and then, due to a perturbing laser field, it transitions into a rotational excited state where the Rydberg states of all three atoms become strongly interacting and ultimately results in the formation of a molecular bond. The conditions required for molecule formation are more stringent for spin-arose states compared to spin-singlet states. Additionally, specific optimal parameters for laser intensity and atom density are determined that maximize the chances of molecule formation. The conditions under which two-body recombination occurs are compared to those required for three-body recombination.

Traditional smoothed particle approximation methods have a inherent limitation in resolving large density variations, which can affect the accuracy of simulations, especially in complex systems with significant changes in density. We've developed a multi-resolution framework for smoothing kernels to address these issues, which incorporates both homogeneous and heterogeneous smoothing kernels to accommodate small and large density changes. We've thoroughly tested the method by conducting multiple convergence studies using different approaches, ultimately verifying its effectiveness in reducing computational costs while maintaining accurate results. We've also applied this method to model interactions between multiple components and moving rigid bodies, demonstrating its suitability for such complex systems.

We utilize a quantum processor to implement a fundamental machine learning algorithm called K-Means clustering. This algorithm groups similar data points into distinct categories represented by the mean value of each subset. By working with a quantum processor, we found that its performance compared to classical models depends heavily on the number of data features. Specifically, gains in terms of computation speed and accuracy tend to decrease as the number of features increases. To address this limitation, we developed a new strategy called guided learning, where the data is pre-processed to reduce its dimensions to a more manageable range, while also employing a quantum-inspired method to determine the optimal number of clusters. Furthermore, we found that guiding the learning process significantly minimizes the loss in terms of computation speed when compared to classical models. Our research involves conducting an experimental study on a quantum hardware platform known as the Rigetti Quantum Cloud Simulator, where we work with different numbers of qubits and repeat the same experiments multiple times to account for statistical variability.

A recent improvement to the FastPitch text-to-speech model has been implemented, specifically designed to enhance pitch control. Initially, the PreNet, which handles pitch variations, was trained alongside the rest of the model. However, this approach proved insufficient, so an alternative method was explored, involving the PreNet being trained separately from the rest of the model using a dataset rich in timbral characteristics. This revised approach resulted in substantially improved results, with the ability to produce more varied and intuitive pitch changes within a given speaker voice.

This study addresses spatiotemporal action recognition by employing a multi-hop
approach within a transformer architecture. The proposed Hopper model leverages
short-term motion and multi-frame velocity information from long-term motion
patterns, also known as gait, to enhance its recognition capabilities. By using
self-attention and cross-attention mechanisms, Hopper achieves significant improvements
over long gait inference methods, with results showing that it handles missing
frames and tempo changes more effectively. Hopper's performance in spatiotemporal
action recognition is demonstrated through experiments on the BCN-PedPhase, BCN-SAT,
DGCOSAR, GW-2D2D, and USC-VISC datasets. With further pre-training and adaptive
frame skipping, Hopper achieves the state-of-the-art in multi-hop spatiotemporal
action recognition. The project's implementation can be found at GitHub using the
handle 'gul820'.

This paper presents an empirical method for extracting the $W$ boson mass from the latest Tevatron collisions, specifically through the process $p\bar{p} \to W \ell \nu b\bar{b}$. The analysis relies on a shape-based approach using $\ell^+ \ell^-$ pairs in the electron channel to build the $m_{\ell \nu}$ distribution, thereby determining the $W$ boson mass. Additionally, an insight into how to assess systematic uncertainties related to shower shower matching is offered, as these affect template construction in this process. The resulting $W$ boson mass is then combined with existing LHC results within a weighted average. The contribution emphasizes that precision measurements at the Tevatron have significant implications for validating the Standard Model, particularly in the context of electroweak precision physics.

Remote-controlled vehicles known as Telepresence robots have gained attention in various fields, thanks to advancements in technology and reduced costs. In the field of psychology, these robots have also been used in experiments involving perception of quality and experience, or Quality of Experience. This study proposes a unique method of measuring QoE for Telepresence robots operated via a virtual reality system. The system allows multiple users to remotely control the robot using virtual controllers, resulting in a key factor influencing QoE: the level of coordination required in the operation. The lack of clear guidelines for measuring the necessary levels of coordination in interactive QoE has been a significant gap in knowledge. To address this, an experiment was conducted with 28 participants, using a combination of questionnaires and an evaluation preview test to develop a scale with four categories of required coordination. The experiment was then repeated with 41 participants to develop a corresponding scale with 20 scenarios. The results showed that the proposed method of measuring QoE for Telepresence robots resonated with users, with ratings above 4 on a 5-point scale. The experiment provided initial insights into the effect of coordination on QoE, suggesting a positive correlation between the two. Furthermore, the study found significant effects of distance, interface, and robot factors on QoE, consistent with existing research. The experiment also highlighted the effects of teamwork and the initial expectations of the experience on QoE. Although not as statistically significant, the study suggested possible relationships between factors such as

In educational measurement, modeling is utilized to customize and adjust assessments in accordance with various groups within the population, which is known as subgroup modeling. A type of analysis model that meets this requirement is the Bayesian hierarchical linear model. This paper provides an accessible introduction to this type of model, including its formulation and the innovative use of Bayesian methods for estimation. Furthermore, developments have been made to this basic model type, including the use of informative priors and model selection techniques. Additionally, this paper will examine various estimation algorithms, focusing on those incorporating Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling and optimization, as well as those generating posterior summaries. To help non-experts understand and implement these models, this paper will present example code using Python, particularly with the Stan and emcee libraries, to build a fundamental Bayesian hierarchical linear model tailored for subgroup analysis in educational assessment.

The game of Mafia involves players taking on specific roles, with a particular objective: some players aim to eliminate others, while a select few aim to survive. We have developed a straightforward mathematical model to study this game, using probability theory to calculate the survival chances of the Lawful or Criminal players. This model works by iteratively eliminating players, with the Lawful players using a specified strategy to eliminate a fixed number of Criminal players at a set interval. We have derived key results, such as a condition for the survival of all players and the maximum number of Criminal players that can be safely eliminated by the Lawful players without risking their own survival. We have also obtained the conditions under which both the Lawful and Criminal players have a non-zero chance of survival. Additionally, our model can be expanded to include games with an irregular playing area and games where the Lawful and Criminal players are eliminated at different intervals.

This study examines how two Jupiter-like planets in a close proximity to each other affects their long-term mass accumulation and the behavior of a surrounding gas and dust disk. It investigates how a fixed amount of gas accretion is split between the conjoined and isolated planets as well as their influence on a surrounding disk, with a focus on how it develops into a disk with distinct inner and outer regions. With a high degree of planetary migration, a gas disk with a high iron content is produced. However, when planets develop near their final positions by a process called orbital resonance migration, a distinctive planet arrangement occurs. Further investigations via a series of interactive and semi-analytical models reveal a pattern, observed in all simulations, where a conjoined planet consistently accretes less mass than two isolated planets, while also promoting more efficient accretion in a surrounding disk. Consequently, if a conjoined planet is not divided, it ends up less massive than two isolated planets, initially reducing the number of planets that eventually become and remain in the category of gas giants. When a conjoined planet is formed near its final location after a series of migrations, it tends to be ejected or sent into an elliptical orbit. With a series of interactions, a gas disk is produced that contains less dust than in typical planetary systems observed.

The electrical conductivity of a single-walled carbon nanotube film was investigated through a variety of methods, including differential resistance measurements as a function of temperature and electric field. The results showed that at low temperatures, the film's resistance exhibited distinct changes at certain electric fields that corresponded to the excitation of specific optical phonony modes. These changes in resistance also aligned with the electronic bandgap of individual nanotubes. Furthermore, the experiment demonstrated that a temperature-dependent electrical conductivity characteristic of one-dimensional systems was observable at higher temperatures, while a three-dimensional conductivity model fit the data collected at room temperature. Our findings indicate the presence of intertube electronic conduction mediated by phonon effects.

This research develops a novel fuzzy k-means approach to cluster high-dimensional data across multiple subspaces. The algorithm is specifically designed for high-dimensional data sets where features may vary in relevance and relevance patterns can shift across subspaces. Building on a previous entropy-based weighted fuzzy k-means method, we refined the initialization process and clustering calculations in an entirely entropy-focused framework. Evaluations on selected datasets demonstrate the superiority of this method compared to traditional fuzzy k-means and several contemporary fuzzy clustering techniques.

The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model has been the primary structure for structured sparse models since its introduction in 1996, including notable variants such as Distributed Gaussian Mixture Models and Hierarchical Neural Attention. Unfortunately, due to its inherent bimodality, training algorithms for MoE models are often prone to instability, leading to suboptimal solutions and significant discrepancies between the expected and actual partitioning results. To address this limitation, we present the first family of consistent MoE learning algorithms that guarantee convergence to optimal solutions. Our new direct learning framework enables the computation of exact posterior probabilities and model weights through an optimization problem, yielding a unique and unique maximum-a-posteriori solution. Our algorithms can be applied to a range of problems, including the classic k-means and k-medians problems, as well as hierarchical and distributed clustering tasks. Our experiments involve clustering static and streaming data using MoE neural networks, and we evaluate both the model weights and partitioning performance. Our findings show that our algorithms produce consistent results, are computationally efficient, and yield superior performance in comparison to the existing state-of-the-art solutions.

This set of notes offers a standalone overview of the theory of chip-firing games on metric graphs along with the theory of Jacobians and Prym varieties, stemming from the 2022 Cambridge summer school on combinatorial methods in algebraic geometry.

We examine how matter behaves in fields exceeding the Planck threshold using an experimental approach distinct from the Standard Model. Our analysis centers on how light behaves when passing through tokyoite and jadeite crystals, which exhibit significant and measurable refractive effects due to the crystals' natural fields exceeding the Planck constant. These measurements lead to two key outcomes. Firstly, we establish a lower limit on the range of a hypothetical graviton, with its minimum length exceeding typical crystal dimensions by several orders of magnitude. Secondly, we find a maximum speed limit for physical processes slightly below the speed of light, with this limit narrowly exceeding the speed of light by less than 0.0000001%. These outcomes provide valuable insights into theories beyond the Standard Model, particularly those involving quantum gravity and forces beyond the reach of current experiments.

Our research presents new findings based on far ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the globular cluster NGC 4147 obtained with three specific filters. These data were further supported by existing proper motion studies, which allowed us to isolate FUV-emitting blue straggler stars (BSS) and a larger group of younger FUV-bright stars within the cluster. Building on prior studies, our results indicate that about 17 to 23 stars in NGC 4147 can be classified as BSS, accounting for roughly 10-18% of the cluster's total blue horizontal branch stars. Our FUV observations also revealed 23 new candidate BSS in NGC 4147, increasing the total count to 38 members, suggesting that BLs make up around 20% of the cluster's total blue horizontal branch stars. In a surprising discovery, our FUV observations indicate that younger stars and BLs dominate the cluster's UV spectrum, outnumbering BSS. These findings imply that young stars, rather than BSS, predominate in shaping the UV luminosity in NGC 4147, a phenomenon also observed in other globular clusters. To understand the origin of the young population in globular clusters, our research explores statistical probabilities and suggests that within the last 50 million years, multiple stellar sub-clusters from the surrounding field merged with NGC 4147.

A key concept known as the b-principle enables the reduction of problems involving Banach space valuations to more manageable problems involving structural instability indices. This study aims to illustrate the principle's applicability to topological problems, specifically by demonstrating that the Mumford Conjecture for hyperbolic surfaces can be framed in terms of a simpler query about the characteristics of certain structural binomial valuations. These binomial valuations have connections to the properties of critical groupoids of binary valuations, a concept related to the fundamental ideas of Cohen, Sanders, and Yurkevicina from 2020.

Deep neural networks' transferability has garnered significant attention in the field of deep learning. Generally, it is thought that a network trained on one dataset can be utilized as a feature extractor for another, with similar or dissimilar categories, and that ongoing training can refine features tailored to the specific dataset. However, we argue that these "two agreements" are flawed. The first one implies that a pre-trained network's existing features are exempt from changes during the subsequent training process, which is clearly incorrect. Indeed, we prove mathematically that an optimal pre-trained feature can evolve into a suboptimal feature. Furthermore, this occurrence is likely to happen in real-world situations. The second agreement suggests that a network trained on a different dataset can yield beneficial features for the new dataset. We contradict this by presenting a scenario in which a network trained on one dataset to extract features for another performs poorly compared to a network trained from scratch. Our findings are supported by experiments set with the benchmark CIFAR-100 dataset. Our work sheds light on the underlying reality of transfer learning, ultimately limiting its expectations.

In various scenarios, such as mobilization and disease spread, the rate of information or entity spread significantly impacts the final outcome, and understanding this rate has far-reaching consequences. For example, in the case of a pandemic, identifying how and at what speed the disease will spread can lead to more targeted resource allocation. Likewise, in social movements, knowing the rate at which information spreads can aid in predicting their success and providing support. Researchers have created models simulating both targeted and tidal breaches, but a universal mathematical description for such rates is still lacking. We propose that a network's structure, particularly its level of organization and the connections between different segments, influences the rate of information spread. By using numerical simulations, we found that a measure of network segmentation is directly associated with the rate of information spread. Moreover, we observed that when a network becomes more fragmented, this leads to a lower rate of spread but also enables a more focused spread, whereas a less organized network, although allowing for a faster spread, results in a more widespread yet inefficient dissemination of information.

We establish a quantitative form of the Thomas-Yau distinctiveness by leveraging a virtual cycle. The proof involves the construction of a 1-dimensional virtual cycle, known as the `Yau tangle', derived from explicit singularities. The Yau tangle is distinct if and only if the original cycle is distinct. By accounting for singularities, we develop a unique ordering on the Yau tangle, confirming the unique nature of each distinct critical point. In addition, we employ tangles to quantify distinctiveness, enabling us to trace explicit singularities and define points of distinctiveness in a graph. We utilize these definitions to analyze the distinctiveness of 1-pointed cubic hypersurfaces and semi-simple symplectic quotients.

The reliability of wireless communication is heavily influenced by time-discrete signal transmission. This work builds on the existing regular perturbation model for modeling effects like phase noise and carrier recovery errors in unamplified wireless links. The model previously established in continuous time, is extended to accommodate discrete-time systems. This transformation necessitates the continuous mapping of the signal-to-snoise ratio (SNR), currently defined in terms of the energy per bit to noise power ratio, to account for the reciprocal bandwidth. Additionally, mathematical expressions are developed to represent the probability of error and link reliability, using the logarithmic decay of the SNR as the power law. This is demonstrated to be a more precise representation than the original model. Furthermore, the increased precision of discrete-time precision analysis is highlighted through comparison to the original model in a specific example, specifically in ultra-wideband communication. This research will ultimately facilitate the accurate assessment of transmission link reliability in discrete-time wireless systems.

The widespread adoption of smartphones has significantly altered how we interact with information. As a result, the security of these devices has become a pressing concern, prompting numerous research efforts in the academic community. Within the mobile domain, a specific attack has been a major focus of study, known as evasion attacks. These particular assaults aim to bypass detection by injecting malicious software into mobile app stores, thus evading detection by security mechanisms. This research aims to provide an comprehensive overview of evasion attacks within the Android operating system. We will explore the internal workings of these attacks, detail past studies, and examine the impact of these threats, culminating in a discussion of open challenges and potential areas of study.

Modern cluster scheduling and management systems are increasingly relying on container technologies like Kubernetes. While these systems excel at deployment, there's a gap when it comes to orchestrating the underlying compute resources. This leads to an additional layer of virtualization, which hinders performance and complicates resource allocation. To bridge this gap, we propose Ozy, a universal orchestration container that bridges the gap between cluster scheduling and hardware resources, offering efficient deployment, and enhanced performance through direct hardware access. By integrating with existing tools like Slurm and Kubernetes/OpenShift, Oazy demonstrates improved efficiency, ease of use, and features a lightweight design with minimal features. With its lightweight architecture, Oazy achieves up to a 3-fold speed boost in jobs, as demonstrated in comparative tests with Kubernetes and Slurm standalone systems.

Recent notable reentries in detailed theoretical constructions of ground states of interacting two-dimensional electron gases in magnetic fields have sparked a growing interest in understanding the underlying physical reality. A notable occurrence is a specific phase of the fractional quantum Hall effect where, for an intermediate level mixing, the entire phase diagram undergoes a reversal of its structure, leading to an unusual reentry into quantized ground states that were initially present in the limit of weak magnetic fields. In this work, we demonstrate that this unique phenomenon is unique to composite fermions moving in a specific type of non-uniform magnetic field that is characterized by a specific change in its structure. A crucial factor in understanding this observation is that the energy of the composite fermions is moderately affected by the variation in Landau-level mixing, an effect that cannot be accounted for by simplified theoretical approaches relying on either strong or weak magnetic fields. Instead, it's possible to create a comprehensive ground-state phase diagram by employing a precise numerical technique, which takes into consideration that the energy of the composite fermions is moderately affected by the variation in Landau-level mixing. A detailed examination of this phase diagram reveals that it incorporates an unusual reentrant phase of the fractional quantum Hall effect where multiple quantized phases coexist in an unexpected manner for an intermediate level mixing.

Our analysis reveals that the conditions necessary for a cosmological black hole, including negative curvature and causality constraints, cannot be met by the Thakurta metric. Furthermore, even setting aside these issues, the equations defining this metric appear to be inconsistent. As a result, the Thakurta metric is ineffective in its intended application of proposing the existence of primordial black holes with unique properties. If such a model were true, it would allow us to set a lower bound on the overall abundance of these black holes based on the observations from the LIGO-Virgo gravitational wave collaboration.

The formation of planets through pebble accretion is supported by simulations of gas-rich protoplanetary disks. However, these predictions haven't been validated by observations of young stars due in part to underlying assumptions in the calculations. One assumption, for example, is that the dust and gas in the disk are uniformly mixed. A new model we suggest makes the reasonable assertion that the dust and gas in the disk are separated, with dust concentrated in the outer regions due to external influences. We calculated the density of the gas and dust at different distances from the star, taking into account their mutual attractions and the external influences. We found a fivefold variation in the mass of planets formed at different distances, a result that initially seemed to disagree with observations of planets. However, when we took into account the fact that the disk we observed was relatively old and calm compared to the planets we predict, the results were more plausible.

In this study, we examine two models - one for predicting functions given partial data and an artificial neural network with limited computational capacity, and another for generating functions given total data and an artificial neural network without operational restrictions. We establish a direct relationship between these models by showing that: (i) there are scenarios in which the predictive model struggles to achieve optimal performance in the generative model; (ii) we develop methods for converting predictions made by the predictive model into meaningful outcomes in the generative model; and (iii) our analysis reveals a correlation between the performance of the predictive model and the efficiency of its simulated counterpart. This similarity in behavior between the predictive and generative models allows us to draw insights into the complexities of the original task by studying them within the more controllable generative model. Our findings shed light on a key requirement for successfully leveraging simulations in predictive tasks - that the predictive model's performance and simulated outcomes exhibit a high degree of correlation. This phenomenon has been dubbed the "Simulation Convergence Condition." We establish a set of general principles that explain how operational constraints influence predictive performance and derive specific requirements for achieving optimal performance under limited computational resources. Our analysis also reveals a direct relationship between data accessibility and the necessary computational capabilities. We (i) demonstrate that there are tasks for which no solution exists without total data and operational restrictions but is feasible with partial data and simulation; and (ii) show that as operational restrictions decrease, the required data also changes, resulting in an optimal trade-off between

We have established a fundamental criterion that enables the minimization of the measure of Bohr sets, primarily consisting of sets generated by subtracting or adding elements from larger groups. In the case of countable abelian groups with respect to Haar measure, this criterion significantly simplifies a previous set by Bergelson, who had already identified a minimization for the difference of two sets within the same group. Additionally, we have expanded upon an earlier estimation by La Fleur, providing a lower bound for the measure of Bohr sets, primarily consisting of sets generated by adding elements from larger groups.

This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban settings where residents have multiple transportation options at their disposal. To remain competitive, ridepooling services must balance high pool participation rates against minimizing detours for users. We propose a Branch-and-Cut algorithm to tackle this challenge, leveraging insights from established route paths to identify and exclude non-viable solutions, thus enhancing lower-bound estimates for arrival times. Additionally, this technique allows us to introduce new valid inequalities that accelerate the optimization process. We conducted an extensive computational analysis involving up to 120 customers and ten vehicles, revealing that our method consistently outperforms a traditional mixed-integer programming formulation by finding significantly more optimal solutions and tighter bounds.

We develop multi-modal pretraining models that incorporate e-commerce domain knowledge to enhance their understanding of categories, brands, and keywords. To this end, we create a large knowledge graph containing over 112K nodes and 288K edges that categorize over 73K brands into 177 categories. Utilizing this graph, we design a pretraining framework that leverages node and edge attention to update large-scale multimedia datasets and thereby improve the accuracy of categories, brands, and keywords. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our proposed method. When integrating this model into existing retrieval algorithms, it demonstrates superior performance on real e-commerce datasets, achieving 12.0% and 27.9% increases in accuracy for brand and category retrieval, respectively. Our pretraining method and knowledge graph framework are openly available to facilitate research and development in the e-commerce field.

A significant characteristic of neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's is the gradual disruption of normal communication within the brain. In early stages of the disease, some neural pathways remain intact, while others start to deteriorate. By utilizing functional MRI (fMRI) technology, researchers can track the progression of these changes and identify which neural pathways are affected. A critical challenge in diagnosing Alzheimer's is effectively utilizing these changes for predictive modeling. A novel approach called DiffMax has been developed to create detailed maps of structural changes in brain tissue via unsupervised learning. By leveraging DiffMax, deep learning networks can learn to identify and differentiate between intact and disrupted neural pathways, significantly improving classification rates. Moreover, by extracting and analyzing volume and location information, the underlying causes of these changes can be understood at a histopathological level.

This study tackles the challenge of understanding simple text meanings by proposing an innovative, efficient deep learning model known as Interaction-based Recurrent Neural Network (IRNN). By incorporating interaction graphs and integrating the outcomes through a process called composition, the proposed architecture generalizes beyond existing recurrent neural networks. Experimental evaluations on various text corpora demonstrate the superiority of our proposed architecture, achieving superior performance in predicting the ensuing text based on given premises. Furthermore, an analysis of the model's performance across diverse corpora reveals its robustness and capacity to perform well on both classical and natural language understanding benchmarks.

The relationship between the orbital and spin of electrons is described using the effective augmented spin-orbit coupling in systems with interacting electrons. We examine the impact of electron interactions on this effect in a pseudospin degenerate band of a strong correlation metal. By establishing a link to the underlying lattice structure through the local magnetic field, we find that in systems with interacting electrons, the spin-orbit coupled pseudospin texture is tied to the antiferromagnetic order. We investigate how this effect influences the formation of local magnetic fields and spin textures near the Fermi level, as well as the behavior of electrons in this region. Our study focuses on the application to superconducting BaNi$_{2}$Pb$_3$ that lacks inversion symmetry.

We explore an Asymptotically Safe model involving Shadow Matter, which remains invisible to conventional Einstein gravity but interacts through a conformal linkage. Introducing Shadow Kennedy-Thorndyke gravity as a replacement for the standard model, we delve into the Kennedy-Thorndyke field's duality in relation to gravitational fields, establishing that graviton shadow antimatter gives rise to a background that resembles de Sitter space. A thorough examination of this theory's cosmological and structural implications yields insights into dark energy, dark matter, and the universe's large-scale properties. Evidence suggests that this theory may resolve the cosmological constant problem while producing a stable cosmological model with inherent plausibility features.

To ensure that AI-powered medical devices operate safely and efficiently in real-world settings, pinpointing their performance levels during evaluation is crucial. Unlike traditional methods for assessing classification models, our approach focuses on estimating reliability metrics, particularly true positive rates and false alarm rates, by leveraging conformal prediction in cases of distribution shifts. Given that reliability metrics are inherently robust against distribution changes, our method proves effective for evaluating classification models and AI-powered medical devices under such changes. Through simulation studies and real-world data analysis, we demonstrate the value of our approach by focusing on a clinical case involving shifted data and show how our method compares favorably to other existing methods.

Systematic and controlled variations in molecular structures, whether regular or irregular, are crucial across numerous biological sciences. Molecular dynamics simulations, a computational method for analyzing the movement of atoms, play a crucial role in exploring the space of possible molecular structures. Nevertheless, altering the structure either globally or locally to shift specific parts is challenging due to the necessity for large or small adjustments, respectively. We introduce RSB-Net, a tool that makes use of neural networks to influence the movement of a frozen molecular component, allowing for the simulation of changes at various scales. Using RSB-Net and simulations of DNA, we show that it is possible to simulate an extensive range of conformational changes, surpassing the limitations of traditional simulations. We found that the optimized simulations accurately represented known DNA configurations and demonstrated an extensive exploration of the space of possible conformations. We observed significant improvements in the simulation of long DNA sequences, exceeding the limitations of traditional simulations, and the insights gained from these optimized simulations can help clarify the complex mechanisms behind DNA's structural refinement.

This paper addresses the issue that conventional entropy encoding methods have a limited ability to adapt to changes in data distributions. In response, we introduce a modern technique called Approximate Next-State Encoding (ANS Encoding), which is based on Markov processes and utilizes conditional probabilities to encode data. We provide a rigorous proof demonstrating the effectiveness of our method in accurately representing high-order distributions with minimal loss, subsequently showing its potential to significantly reduce the rate at which information is transmitted. Furthermore, we outline the principles of its implementation, detailing how to determine optimal parameter values. We conduct a study using real-world data to compare its performance to that of the classic Arithmetic and Laplace-based entropy encoding methods.

The dielectric characteristics of the pore solution play a crucial role in understanding various processes in cement-based materials due to their close spatial relationship. However, the dielectric properties of these solutions are not well-documented despite their importance. This study therefore aimed to investigate the dielectric behavior of the pore solution in cement-based materials. A series of experiments were conducted using different concentrations of calcium-based solutions with either osteosarcoma cells or deionized water, and the results were compared to those obtained from measurements on mortar and concrete. Our findings showed that as time progressed, the dielectric properties of these solutions/extracts and cement-based materials/pastes converged. Furthermore, the data suggested that concentrated calcium-based solutions exert a suppressive effect on the dielectric properties, although this effect can be overcome with time. Moreover, it was observed that a wider range of measurements on concrete pastes/pastes can be achieved by studying the dielectric properties of the pore solution.

We review recent research on heavy hadronic molecules composed of quarks and leptons, specifically focusing on the role of light open heavy flavor mesons as constituent parts. Our analysis centers on the characteristics of these heavy ground states and their adjacent resonances, with an emphasis on their underlying dynamics and how they are regulated by hadronic processes. To enhance our understanding, we examine the spectral lines of decay in these heavy composite particles, with a special emphasis on their relations to $X(3872)$, the $\chi_{c1}(3872)$, and other similar particles. Our investigation also explores the theoretical representation of these heavy entities within the context of the quark potential model and further delves into their structural composition by using the resulting parameters in a reduced model based on the quark potential theory. In addition, we review recent discoveries related to massive-heavy hadronic molecules, with an examination of their characteristics and possible interpretations. Our discussion concludes with an examination of future experimental discoveries that could occur in the field of hadronic molecules. To facilitate detection, we generate theoretical decay spectra for the $1D_2 - 3S_1$ transition in $Y(4260)$ as an example of a high-mass state.

Recent research has shown significant interest in the military applications of unmanned swarms. Various organizations are now devoting substantial resources to this dynamic field, which is expected to shape future national security strategies and revolutionize land, air, and maritime operations. Given the numerous possible uses of swarms in different environments and sectors, identifying the specific areas and organizations focusing on military swarm systems proves to be extremely useful for both operational and business purposes. In our analysis, we apply Natural Language Processing techniques to an extensive database consisting of over 76,000 documents from 2020. Our method yields over 680 distinct clusters, including key areas such as naval operations in the Pacific, German military cooperation with other nations, and various military initiatives in the Middle East and Asia.

Hammouma et al. introduced a technique to extract the overall pattern of a proxy cavity's 3D profile using flux data from multiple lines-of-sight. In this research, we apply this approach to data from two sources: MGS and eBOCES, both of which utilize proxy fluctuations at a redshift of approximately $2$. In order to evaluate its effectiveness, several mock simulations are used that model the impact of different levels of discrete absorption patterns, denoted as $C_{2}$. Through this process, the simulated absorption patterns are converted into proxy profiles and compared against the actual data and other comparison methods that measure the correlation function of the data. In this research, we find that my $C_{2}$ reconstruction technique far surpasses the other comparison methods in terms of resolving detail from the data, with a 5 sigma confidence threshold of approximately $3\times10^{-4}$ for proxy profiles and $1.5\times10^{-3}$ for density profiles of the data. In a series of models that explain dark matter and dark energy using proxy profiles and HST luminosity density data, we find that our research indicates that the universe's matter density, denoted as $\Omega_m$, must be in the range of.04 to.6, that is. In contrast, if one were to use the average proxy density directly in the data rather than our more refined technique then the range would be.03 to.8, exhibiting a nearly tenfold

Researchers at the Fermilab Accelerator have successfully demonstrated emittance transfer between transverse and longitudinal beams for the first time. The experiment utilized a specific $e^+e^-$ resonance decaying into light neutral mesons to study the temporal distribution of $e^-$ trajectories. The advanced beam manipulation and detection systems enabled precise measurement of the emittance transfer, which was then analyzed using simulated data to determine the actual value. The resulting outcome agrees with the standard quantum electrodynamic model, confirming our understanding of this phenomenon.

A crucial component of intelligent transportation systems is predicted trajectory information, particularly useful for autonomous vehicles and robots navigating through crowded areas. The predicted trajectories often prove inaccurate, leading to subpar performance, as they fail to account for the dynamic nature of surroundings. In particular, existing deep learning methods and their variants primarily focus on short-term predictions, while neglecting the significance of long-term trajectory direction. In this paper, we introduce a novel method, incorporating socially-aware factors, to enhance both the short and long-term prediction accuracy. The proposed approach relies on a sequence of conditional variational autoencoders to produce a sliding trajectory. By leveraging socially-aware factors such as personal characteristics, head orientation, and eye direction, this method generates refined predictions that consider these social cues. The method achieves significant superiority in trajectory prediction over existing approaches, as evident from the results of our experiments using the Human360 and Crowdsynth datasets, showcasing improved long-term prediction accuracy and reduced forecasting error.

In the realm of artificial neural networks, particularly within Boltzmann machines, our primary objective involves analyzing and evaluating the structural versus statistical complexity. Structural complexity is concerned with the number of hidden units, while statistical complexity is tied to the specific organization of the units. To assess this complexity, we utilize information-theoretic metrics such as mutual information, conditional mutual information, and total correlation. Our research differs from prior studies in the following ways, as it focuses on examining the variations of these metrics in response to altering the number of hidden units, rather than fixing it, and in learning versus generative processes, rather than leveraging previously obtained knowledge. Additionally, we also expand upon the existing analysis of BM by investigating the variations of our metrics in response to alterations in training versus validation processes, which enables us to gain insight into how these metrics change in response to adjusting both the structural and statistical aspects of the model.

This trial focuses on the development of techniques that enable swarms of robots to interact with human leaders in a decentralized manner. We introduce a novel hand signal recognition method based on sequential patterns, specifically designed for the detection of intentions in swarms navigating through complex environments. Our proposed approach employs a Gaussian Mixture Model to analyze the swarm's velocity and direction, distinguishing between three distinct state patterns: global, following, and leading states. We tested the method using a human-guided quadcopter swarm, assessing its effectiveness with various hand signal presentation rates and durations in both static and dynamic environments. The results demonstrate the method's potential for accurately identifying the swarm's state, even when human leaders employ suboptimal hand signal strategies. Furthermore, we examine the influence of hand signal rate and duration on human-swarm collaboration, investigating the limitations and opportunities for decentralized interaction.

The study aims to assess how ensembling neural networks can classify white and red blood cells in images, specifically using the 2018 ISIC challenge dataset. Two main ensembling methods were explored: merging classifications from trained networks and merging trained networks' weights. It was found that the merged classifications method excels at accurately identifying red blood blood cells. Conversely, the merged weights method tends to perform better in classification tasks, particularly when dealing with red blood blood cells. Surprisingly, combining classified samples did not lead to overall improvement. It was observed that the merged classifications method can likely be improved by retraining the networks rather than merging them. Moreover, the success of the merged weights method suggests that the primary factor contributing to classification is the networks' ability to accurately locate key features in images, rather than their ability to correctly classify samples.

A key advantage of counterdiabatic protocols in driving quantum states involves the use of a supporting, often complex extra gauge potential. However, incorporating this potential into real-time quantum driving methods is often difficult due to high computational costs. A new approach in this paper achieves a simplified, efficient gauge potential for a family of models that can be effectively represented by nearest-neighbor interactions. Furthermore, this efficient approach also enables an optimized, efficient driving method for these models, using variational quantum simulation and real-time evolution to reproduce the target Hamiltonian's ground state. Experimentation with a four-site Hubbard model and quantum simulator demonstrates the method's efficiency.

This research presents a novel color image processing method that mimics the way human vision experiences gradual changes in color over space and time. A basic input image is enhanced through a simple operation that optimizes its brightness, then further transformed using an innovative color correction technique based on color temperature. By applying distinct color temperatures to different regions of the image, our method efficiently replicates the natural shifts in color we see in our surroundings. This results in an interesting, futuristic look that is ideal for various film and visualization applications, especially those involving high-dynamic range content. Unlike other multi-band processing techniques, our method can be implemented quickly and efficiently because it involves minimal image segments. This makes it an excellent choice for time-critical applications or those requiring hardware optimization. Unlike other techniques that rely on pre-defined patterns or algorithms, our approach is highly customizable. A set of empirical guidelines for adjusting the method's key parameters is provided, allowing artists and developers to apply this technique to their work. Our paper includes a series of experimental examples demonstrating how this method can be used to create a range of interesting visual effects, from subtle color changes to more extreme transformations.

This work investigates the behavior of a parameter-dependent function, $f(\alpha) \exp (-\lambda \alpha^2)$, as $\alpha$ approaches positive infinity, focusing on deriving an explicit, parameter-dependent asymptotic expression for its Taylor series expansion about any point $\alpha_0$. Our analytical results are further validated through a developed set of computational methods. These methods can be applied to determine the number of positive real roots of the function $f(\alpha) - y(\alpha)$, where $y(\alpha)$ is a given asymptotic expression, in the practical context of computational mathematics. This is achieved by constructing an error function, $e(\alpha)$, which represents the remaining term in the Taylor expansion, and further computed using a truncated series expansion of the differential equation $f'(\alpha)-y'(\alpha)=2\lambda \alpha e(-\alpha)$. Our approach allows us to asymptotically resolve Gaussian decomposition, which involves decomposing a function $f(\alpha)$ into separate Gaussian components, and we present several significant examples of computing roots and approximating transcendental functions with asymptotic expressions.

Given a surface S equipped with a metric d, such that it meets the conditions set by Alexandrov for an upper curvature bound, we demonstrate that an almost conformal harmonic map from a surface to the pair (S, d) results in a branched covering. Consequently, if (S, d) is topologically equivalent to the two-dimensional sphere S^2, it then becomes conformally equivalent to S^2.

A novel facility utilizing a laser-plasma interaction stage has been suggested for conducting groundbreaking photon-photon collision research. The suggested concept takes inspiration from physical principles underlying both free-electron lasers and laser-plasma interactions. The FE-LP approach leverages the natural occurrence of high-field plasma areas within the beam waist of a self-amplified free-electron laser, where intense laser-plasma interactions can produce extraordinary electromagnetic fields, thereby enabling truly strong-field QED phenomena driven by interaction between intense laser light and high-density plasma. The unique environment of this facility allows for the simultaneous utilization of particle beams, intense laser light, and electromagnetic fields to achieve groundbreaking research in photon-photon collisions, including the production of photonuclear reaction pairs, real gamma-ray production from particle collisions, and relativistic laser-plasma interactions, thereby opening new avenues in fields such as nuclear physics, material science, and astrophysics. Additionally, the facility could serve as an interdisciplinary research hub, bridging areas such as laser-plasmas, particle physics, nuclear physics, astrophysics, and solid-state physics, thereby promoting interdisciplinary education and training.

In a forthcoming publication, we will present a comprehensive analysis of the constraints imposed by the Higgs boson and electroweak precision data on a 2HDM model with a truncated Yukawa structure, specifically when one of its components is negligible. Here, we highlight a critical observation relevant to model building: this structure is unique in ensuring that one of the Yukawa interactions is non-vacuum invariant, provided another coupling is nearly invariant under a continuous symmetry. Notably, this discovery has significant implications for a wide variety of doublet-doublet models that feature a distinctive, non-diagonal Yukawa interaction. Furthermore, this implication has a substantial impact on model building, as it enables a straightforward calculation of the constraint imposed by the Higgs boson mass on the model's other key parameter. In particular, this constraint is substantial, corresponding to approximately 10% of the new physics scale, for an ideal alignment of Higgs couplings to both fermions and gauge bosons. In contrast, the constraint is much more stringent, corresponding to a substantial fraction of the new physics scale, when the Higgs boson couplings to fermions are misaligned relative to the standard model or when the trilinear gauge couplings have different expectations based on their corresponding tree-level values.

Resource Description Framework (RDF) data represents information in a graph format based on concepts like subjects, properties, and values, providing compatibility with various query languages such as SPARQL. The RDF data model's advantages have led to its usage across diverse domains; however, its applicability is restricted to datasets adhering to its specification. To facilitate data conversion from alternative formats to RDF graphs, the problem of aligning resource representations must be addressed. Recent initiatives like Shape Expression (SHAPE) have aimed at defining and governing the structure of RDF data, enabling machine-readable data constraints and formalized validation. Our work extends SHAPE profiles by introducing a schema transformation technique, which enables the conversion of Relational Data Models to RDF graphs compliant with specified Shape Expression profiles.

A dataset's shape information can greatly impact the results of statistical analysis, yet conventional tools often neglect this crucial element, focusing solely on summary statistics like means and variances. The StoNED algorithm, developed by Kratz and Ronchetti in 2004, uses kernel density estimation to create a shape-based model, which combines with a location parameter estimate to form a complete model. By incorporating this model into the popular StoNED estimation, which is itself an adaptation of the NED algorithm, NED ESTimation provides accurate and robust estimations, even in the presence of outliers. Built upon the widely used Python hydrology library pypop, our pyStoNED package offers a user-friendly set of functions to create, save, and optimize various types of StoNED-related datasets and graphs.

In the Note, we examine the simultaneous analysis of associated top quark pairs and a charged Higgs boson at the LHC, focusing on the $t \bar t \phi$ production mode. This combines with existing $t \bar t \phi$ production data to enable a more comprehensive sensing of the $\phi$-related parameters. Our results show that significant sensitivity to $\phi$-related parameters can be achieved, significantly improving the bounds on these parameters when data on charged Higgs boson production is included. This combines with existing $t \bar t \phi$ production data to enable a more precise estimation of these parameters. Assuming the mass of the charged Higgs boson is less than 320 GeV, our findings reveal that its mass can be estimated with a 10% margin of error after analyzing available LHC data.
