Nonetheless, the resulting high-dimensional data is difficult to compress efficiently, which hinders its practical applications. To address this challenge, we propose a novel method for compressing light field images, using a learning-based approach that incorporates a sophisticated statistical model of image parallax effects. Our compression framework consists of three interconnected components: a novel image parallax effect model, a geometric transform module, and a entropy coding method. The image parallax effect model enables accurate prediction of images within a given viewing angle, while the geometric transform module generates compact low-rank representations of predicted images, extracting additional detailed information from these images. Our entropy coding method efficiently encodes the remaining information required by the discrete cosine transform (DCT) model. By combining a DCT model with our newly developed methods, we achieve superior compression performance, particularly in terms of structural retention. Our approach has practical implications for capturing full 3D scenes using light field technology. Thorough qualitative and quantitative assessments demonstrate the efficacy of our compression framework, which significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of compression ratio and image quality.

The effectiveness of interactive and non-interactive models in cross-language information retrieval using dense vector embeddings has been explored and compared in this research. Interactive models, trained with annealing techniques, outperform non-interactive models like Multlingual BERT in tasks such as CLIR. However, their complex nature makes them difficult to deploy and prone to overfitting due to hyperparameter tuning sensitivity. To improve on these limitations, this study modified the Annealing Cross-Lingual Retrieval model by merging it with non-interactive multlingual BERT and implementing a novel adaptive scheduling technique for temperature adjustment. Our findings indicate significant performance gains from the proposed modifications. Moreover, this study conducts a cost analysis of ACLRet's performance and discovers that effective search results can be achieved even with early stopping even at relatively low computational costs.

The urgent need for precise poverty estimates has driven the expansion of small-area estimation methods within big data platforms like mobile phone surveys and Geographic Information Systems. Researchers are now faced with an overwhelming variety of sophisticated algorithms drawing from big data sources. This study aimed to determine the feasibility of employing survey-weighted statistical techniques on small scales, particularly in low and middle income countries, using both synthetic and real world datasets. A country-level poverty map was created from a mobile phone survey in Kenya, utilizing 1km2 Geographic Information Systems data. A comparison of estimations using various techniques revealed the limitations of many design-based methods in creating detailed poverty maps. A models-based approach, combining Bayesian shrinkage techniques and latent variable modeling, produced the most accurate results. This method can effectively integrate disparate data sources, such as surveys and Geographic Information Systems, even with limited data availability.

Inspired by the success of Kelly wagering in traditional and quantum contexts, we seek to develop a similar strategy for betting with quantum systems that utilize continuous variables. To this end, we define a new betting approach based on a quantum estimator derived from the Kiefer-Wolfowitz unbiased estimator, which effectively conveys the true mean of a variable. Our estimator is capable of being updated in an incremental manner with minimal computational requirements. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this quantum estimator maintains the same optimal performance as its classical counterpart. Building on this, we devise a Kelly-like betting protocol for continuous variable systems, in which a quantum state is shared between two parties, facilitating a mutually unbiased estimation of a variable. Our protocol enables the simultaneous harvesting of statistical benefits by both participants as the variable's value becomes known. The proposed betting protocol exhibits robustness in the presence of decoherence and achieves a superior success rate in a realistic simulation model.

The recently created compound semiconductors MoSi$_2$N$_4$, MoGe$_2$N$_4$, WSi$_2$N$_4$, WSi$_2$P$_4$, TiSi$_3$N$_2$, TiGe$_2$N$_4$, and their various counterparts have been identified due to their unique properties and stable ranges of band gaps. By employing density functional theory, we have conducted an in-depth exploration of their electronic structures, with special attention to the arrangement of bands resulting from the stacking of layers. It is revealed that the band arrangement is not significantly affected by the type of stacking. Furthermore, a consistent set of band parameters applies to all compounds with a certain type of stacking. The Mo-based compounds, in contrast, exhibit a distinct band topologically distinct from the others, owing to their unique orbital configuration, whereas the others form a coherent category. The Mo-based compounds are predicted to be viable candidates for efficient thermophotonic applications due to their large and adjustable excitonic effects, thereby expanding the potential uses of these compound semiconductors.

The search for exotic decays of the $\Sigma^+$ particle has been conducted using the LHCb experiment's proton-proton collision data, which amount to 3 $ \rm{fb}^{-1} $ at a 13 TeV energy level. A significant outcome after examining the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^- $ decay is the discovery of a first-ever observation with a frequency of $4.2 \pm 1.1 \pm 0.4 \pm 0.1 \times 10^{-8}$, where multiple sources of uncertainty are involved. Furthermore, this discovered rate is consistent with the predictions of the SM, as well as those of the SM's Compton photoproduction process. Also for the first time, the $\Sigma^+ \to p \pi^+ \pi^- $ decay is being reported with a frequency of $11.8 \pm 2.8 \pm 1.3 \pm 0.5 \times 10^{-7}$, where it is primarily caused by the resonant decay $\Sigma^* \to p \pi^- $.

The beginning of a protoplanetary disk formation is a complex event influenced by the dynamics and physical conditions of a prestellar core as it transitions into a Class 0 object. In this study, we employed high-resolution simulations of core collapse and disk formation to study the intricate relationships between protostars and their surrounding disks during the initial formation of a protoplanetary disk. Our model accurately represented the breakdown of a prestellar core and efficiently simulated the disk formation and protostar properties for an extended period. We observed a consistent pattern of a flattened disk appearing within 10,000 years of a prestellar core breaking down. At this stage, the protostar's properties such as mass, luminosity, and terminal velocity of the outflow consistently fell within a narrow range. It became clear that the typical protostar properties reported in observations are a result of an average over a long period of disk formation (at least 10 times longer) than disk existence. Therefore, any observed values represent an average over a long period. Our model also predicted a long-standing disk problem where the accretion exceeds outflow outflow mass by a large margin, and we further explored how the dynamical and chemical changes in a protostar environment affect the typical prestellar core properties as a prestellar core breaks down into a protostellar stage.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current solutions, like ADCs, assume atmospheric conditions based on model analyses, which may not always accurately represent the actual situation. The development of a practical system for on-sight atmospheric dispersion profiling, an adaptation of the LiDAR technique, presented in the initial paper, enables more precise characterization of atmospheric conditions. This subsequent paper outlines the methodology for generating atmospheric models based on the previous paper's results and incorporating them into the ADP system. Moreover, it proposes a strategy for integrating the results of on-sight measurements into atmospheric models, enabling the refinement of atmospheric dispersion models in use.

Energy consumption and industrial production are examples of activities
involving multiple time steps, constrained by capacity limits. The seasonal
variability of such processes often fluctuates around a sparse code
representing its characteristics. This paper proposes a hierarchical Bayesian
model for analyzing multi-period time series that is characterized by sparse
prior distributions in one stage and superposition of mixed Gaussian
distributions in another. By utilizing the variational approximation, we derive
a structured variational inference approach, which yields a posterior that
maintains sparsity at multiple time steps. Our model's efficiency is verified
by conducting simulations on artificially generated data and comparing it to
other methods. Furthermore, we apply our proposed model to the Natural
Gas consumption time series in New England and the Industrial production
time-series from US, demonstrating its ability to uncover hidden factors.

In a Stone space, specifically in a compact one, the Stone topology has a relationship reminiscent of a Pontryagin duality principle when applied to its lattice of subsets, which can be utilized to formulate a dual relationship with the lattice of ultrafilters within it. This interaction can be categorized using a constant logic framework, which also facilitates an interpretation of compact abelian groups within this context. This duality is exemplified through an analysis of the Stone spaces corresponding to $[0;1]$ and the unit disk $D$, where the topology of the former is dual to the topology of the latter in a particular context.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts utilize fairness metrics and data protection techniques such as differential privacy (DP) in their research. A promising approach, known as federated learning (FL), utilizes a client-server architecture to combine the effectiveness of deep learning with enhanced ethics and security. At its core, FL is a distributed computing framework that enables secure collaboration between participants by safeguarding their private information. To expedite model development, FL often employs consensus algorithms such as Federated Averaging (FA), but this process is compromised in settings requiring DP. Moreover, we discover that even when conforming to DP, certain types of bias can still persist in the trained models. We demonstrate this by showing that bias can sometimes be transmitted from the raw data to the final model under specific conditions. To mitigate this issue, we analyze a variety of existing fairness metrics and examine the effect of different privacy protocols on them, before proposing an improved variant of the DPFA, which offers superior results for training models under strict data protection protocols while also maintaining high fairness standards.

We've modified a supersymmetric minimal $U(1)_X$ model by introducing a new gauge singlet, the right-handed scalar and two right-handed fermions, which allows for $Z_2$ symmetry and leads to right-handed neutrinos, thereby solving the dark matter issue and providing a new theoretical framework for neutrino dark energy. In our model, we set the first soft supersymmetry mass at 1 TeV, which was previously not feasible due to experimental restrictions on $R$-parity violating couplings. In our analysis, we examine the influence of these constraints on supersymmetric sparticle masses and we show that supersymmetric particles above 1 TeV in mass are consistent with the current LHC results. Furthermore, we have computed the self-coupling of the new gauge boson and we found that supersymmetric particle masses below 10 TeV are achievable in this model, thereby making it a viable candidate at the energy frontier of the LHC. We have also investigated the possible production of a scalar boson in this model and found the lower mass limit of this boson to be 740 GeV, assuming that it decays into the $U(1)_X$ gauge boson and the lightest supersymmetric particle, thereby making it a viable candidate at future experiments. We have also presented the possible impact of this model at 100 TeV pp collider.

In this research, we investigate a wireless powered communication network with a device assisted by an IRS and multiple access, where the energy-harvesting user is affected by interference launched by a single source. To circumvent this issue, an optimized resource allocation plan is introduced, combining semi-deviation techniques and optimization. Specifically, the users' transmission power and the IRS's reflection factor are optimized through an AL algorithm based on a multi-objective problem that increases the total information rate, equates energy harvesting and interference power, and eliminates zero-rate conditions. To further improve the performance of the proposed solution, a DL-based method is developed to refine the AL-generated values over successive iterations. Ultimately, the simulated results show the efficacy of the proposed models, demonstrating the advantages of the users and the performance of the DL model compared to other existing techniques.

For the first time, researchers used total absorption gamma spectroscopy to measure the Gamow-Teller strength distribution in $^{186}$Hg decaying into $^{186}$Au and compared it to theoretical QRPA calculations employing the SLy4 Skyrme force. The measured strength distribution, alongside the nuclei's half-lives, is best explained by incorporating a combination of prolate and oblate configurations independently in the parent and daughter nuclei. Prolate components dominated both parent and daughter nuclei for the experimental beta strength, while an upper limit was set for the oblate component in the parent state. To analyze the data, a minimum of three consecutive beta decay states was required for both progeny orientations, indicating prolate-dominated structures in both. The calculation that accounted for a broad range of QRPA configurations resulted in the calculation of the experimental beta strength, with the exception of the daughter's oblate component, which was not accounted for in the present study. The half-life measured in this study, 87.2 ms, for the $^{186}$Hg beta decay into $^{186}$Au with total absorption gamma spectroscopy, agreed with previous in-flight beta plus decay measurements. The new results, along with the calculation of the daughter's natural parity mix, confirm a normal shape for the $^{186}$Hg beta decay distribution in terms of spin and parity.

We explore the intersection of Dark Subrahmanyan's theory of Dark Matter, known as baryon-motivated dark matter, and the theory of leptogenesis, particularly in models incorporating a common framework. This common framework arises naturally in certain unified theory models and includes a common supermultiplet for neutrinos and dark matter. Our analysis delves into the connection between the two sectors in the common framework and the implications of this connection for Dark Matter and the universe. Specifically, we investigate how the two sectors contribute to the same dark matter particles and how these particles affect baryon asymmetry, dark matter density, and neutrino mass. Our results include constraints from CP violation and the neutrinoless double beta decay for different model variations. One of the variations involves a model similar to a minimal $SO(10)$ model with a $A_4$-symmetric sector, while another involves a model similar to a minimal $SO(10)$ model with a right-handed neutrino-mediated interaction to dark matter, and finally, in the final model, we have a model similar to a minimal $SO(10)$ model with a common Dirac and Majorana neutrino sector.

We've developed a control method that leverages supplementary information to achieve effective results in complex obstacles-ridden control scenarios, even when working with limited data. The approach involves identifying a control policy by solving a high-dimensional optimization problem, which takes into account the available supplementary information. The method's innovation lies in its ability to apply the side information in a unified optimization framework, thereby enhancing the control performance. The approach does not require knowledge of the dynamic model and is adaptable to various types of side information. In addition, it allows the integration of diverse objective functions. We tested the method with a dataset consisting of flight, swimming, reaching, and walking trajectories. The experiments, which involved evaluating the method on a quadruped robot, demonstrated its capability to find optimal control policies in various tasks despite only having a single trial. The results also showed that incorporating different types of side information can significantly improve the method's performance.

In the context of the Toda conformal field theory, specifically with $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ as the underlying Lie algebra, a previously established relationship called the 'Ward relationship' arises within the framework of the free fermionic path integral formulation. This relationship serves as an alternative, more streamlined formulation of the Gao-Qiu-Weng identity, which itself revolves around the partition function of the Toda conformal field theory. As a derivative effect, this identity led to the identification of novel, nontrivial Toda conformal field theory correlation functions, a discovery that leverages the 'Toda hydrodynamics' that describes the 'Toda currents' dynamics, which plays a pivotal role in this investigation.

Recent breakthroughs in GAN research attribute some of the success to relation networks, particularly in enhancing minimax training, although the underlying reasons for these improvements are not well understood. In this research, we investigate the connection between relation networks and GANs by examining how the implementation details impact GAN training. Our findings indicate that while earlier implementations were plausible, a more precise analysis using triplet loss semantics reveals flaws in previous typing conventions. A novel typing convention is introduced, and a more informed approach to implementing relation networks in GANs is developed. Our research leads to the design of a new relation GAN model, and through thorough testing, we confirm that it outperforms existing models across various datasets, including ImageNet and Celeba, ultimately contributing to significant advancements in GAN research through the GAN Baseline Challenge.

A novel approach for practical quantum communication over long-distance fiber has been developed through the implementation of hybrid direct and indirect quantum key exchange methods without securing synchronization of optical phase. This innovative technique utilizes a distinct method for generating, distributing, and managing entangled light beams in a way that avoids the necessity for phase locking, thereby reducing the complexity involved in the process. This complexity reduction serves to significantly improve the performance and efficiency of the process. Furthermore, we have successfully put into practice a new method of fast quantum key exchange negotiation utilizing four intensity detectors, thereby accelerating the entire process and achieving secure key rates exceeding 6 Megabits per second. This breakthrough has paved the way for the implementation of secure quantum communication over long-distance fiber with potentially unprecedented speed and efficiency.

We identify the Toeplitz algebras resulting from classical and weighted versions of the Fock space and Hardy space on the complex plane, utilizing specific symbols that are tied to particular subspaces within these spaces.

Deep learning-based object detection has cements its dominance in object detection tasks, primarily due to its exceptional edge detection capabilities. Nonetheless, it is limited in applying knowledge to situations involving novel objects and scenarios not encountered during its initial training. In order to overcome this limitation, research has used a novel training technique known as 'zero-shot object detection,' offering promising results, even in environments where the coordinates of the objects cannot be precomputed. This type of object detection is known as 'open vocabulary object detection,' and in this study, a method to tackle this challenge under complex circumstances is presented. The method generates pseudo-boundng-box labels in a self-supervised and semi-supervised manner for identification, and results show significant improvements over leading techniques in open vocabulary object detection. Additionally, the integration of pseudo-image labels further enhances its accuracy, and the method has successfully identified 37 out of 41 objects in the GLEAM-D dataset without the need for re-training. The code for this method has been made publicly available on GitHub at the following URL: https://github.com/ExplainableAIResearch/Open-VOC-Bbox-Labels.

A large program using the ALMA telescope has made detailed observations of star formation in the Rho Ophiuchus cloud. Our analysis focused on one specific source, S1, a source surrounded by outflows, thermal gas, and potentially interacting with a nearby photoactive star. Our analysis of the data revealed that the star formation region is composed of three distinct components, each with a unique temperature: 50 Kelvin, 300 Kelvin, and 1000 Kelvin. The colder component likely contains solid particles and has a high density while the warmer region, possibly associated with an outflow, has a much lower density and is dominated by atomic gas. Our observations also indicate that the thermal gas is in contact with the hot 1000 Kelvin region and contains molecular ions. Our model shows that the thermal gas is in equilibrium with the hot region and contains similar ion populations as the hotter region. Our analysis further reveals that the gas is in contact with the central star, (although not directly in front of it), and as a result, the gas is ionized and has its density manipulated by ionized and atomic components. Our model shows that the gas is in the initial stages of being ionized and has not yet been completely ionized through a combination of heated and evaporated material. Our analysis of the gas also indicates the presence of a 1000 Kelvin region that is not observable due to the effects of absorption and suggests further research into the gas' composition and structure.

Deep learning's success has been prominent, with deep neural networks increasing model trust by enhancing their fairness and robustness. However, deep models' high confidence in their predictions often leads to overconfidence, which causes them to make more mistakes. Truthfulness, the opposite aspect of this, is lacking in traditional neural networks, which are often inconsistent in their predictions. In contrast, evidence-based reasoning in human decision-making is rooted in the combination of ability and effort, offering a compelling case for incorporating veracity into machine learning. This article aims to provide an overview of the techniques used to quantify the truthfulness of classification models, specifically focusing on transformers, which have become the go-to model type for various NLP tasks. The article will cover the various measures of truthfulness, classify transformers by their architecture, and quantify the truthfulness of transformer models. It will also explore the truthfulness of pre-trained models and examine how to improve it through training methods, in addition to examining the truthfulness in semi-supervised and active learning scenarios. Furthermore, the article will cover the truthfulness in multiclass problems and the use of truthfulness in downstream tasks.

The performance of portfolio management, including optimal investment allocation and asset pricing, heavily relies on the accuracy of mortality forecasts. Machine learning and statistical modeling have recently been utilized more extensively than before. This study compares the effectiveness of two types of factor models, particularly the regularized principal component regression and the regularized regression model with time-varying factor loadings, using data on social security beneficiaries in the United States. Results indicate that models incorporating time-varying factor loadings consistently achieve superior outcomes across nearly all scenarios. Furthermore, the advantages gained from using time-varying factor loadings are largely due to their ability to mitigate the issues of factor regularization. This study's findings are expected to contribute to the continued advancement of mortality forecasting techniques.

The goal of neural architecture search (NAS) is to automate the design of deep learning models, with solutions increasingly being applied in the wild. Yet, due to the vast number of possible architectures, NAS employs sampling methods and represents them through parameterization, which introduces bias. In this study, we investigate how sampling, parameterization, and resulting bias impact NAS. Focusing on the leading architecture search approach, we develop and evaluate three techniques aimed at minimizing bias introduced by parameterization. Our experiments demonstrate that the common practice of running multiple runs with random samples has mainly served to mask the effects of bias, and that our proposed remedies yield substantial improvements.

Time series analysis is a fundamental component of finance, economics, and signal processing, but the analysis of multivariate time series is often neglected due to the additional complexity it presents. Focusing solely on univariate time series can result in the overlooking of significant information hidden within the relationships between multiple series. This article presents an interactive R package called theft, which provides a comprehensive set of functions for exploring both homogeneous and heterogeneous multivariate time series. The examples demonstrate the distinct advantages of analyzing multiple series together to uncover more valuable insights that may otherwise remain confined to individual series.

This research notes that in an irreducible geodesically complete proper CAT(0) space, 
the following conditions are equivalent: the space has all edges as
locally compact, the space has all edges as compactly embedded, and the space's
unoriented geodesic ball of any non-zero radius contains a geodesic triangle
with an angle at the perimeter that approaches π as it tends to zero.

Human-assisted verification of machine translation outputs is a crucial step in ensuring the quality of translated content. Translators are typically responsible for reviewing and validating these translations. To optimize the translation process, it is crucial to allocate resources effectively by identifying the most challenging domains and adjusting the amount of human verification conducted accordingly. This paper presents an innovative approach based on reinforcement learning to identify the most complex subjects for human review during the translation process. A Bayesian method is employed to determine the reliability of translators in different domains, utilizing two key performance indicators: translation accuracy and consistency with the original text. By providing numerical reliability scores for each domain, this system enables the identification of subjects with the highest risk of errors, thereby informing resource allocation for maximum effectiveness. The proposed method was evaluated using a corpus of 988 samples of parallel texts across four domains, accompanied by human assessments of their reliability. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of this approach, with the model successfully identifying five subjects for human review and accurately mirroring the reliability scores provided by human assessors.

We derive two key principles related to energy transmission through disordered systems. Our first finding establishes a sum of transmission probabilities equal to 1. To obtain this result, we employ a mathematical approach by considering the independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) probabilities of transmission from different channels. In contrast, when each channel's probability of transmission is non-zero and unrelated to its position, we demonstrate that the sum of transmission probabilities at each position is bounded by a specific range. Our methods also apply to the study of quantum systems, where we examine the sum of probabilities of energy deposition into specific states at different detection points.

The concept of "lottery ticket hypothesis" in deep neural networks suggests that by pruning the unessential components of a highly complex, yet overfitting network, it is possible to obtain a more streamlined yet equally accurate sub-network. Our research focuses on assessing the practicality of generating such sub-networks through pruning in two distinct models: one with fully connected layers and another with convolutional layers. By examining the impact of successive pruning phases on both models, we aim to determine which is more suitable for creating high performing yet sparse neural networks. Additionally, we aim to unravel the underlying structural differences between the surviving neurons in these models and elucidate their inherent predictive mechanisms. Our results indicate that by systematically eliminating a calculated percentage of neurons during each phase, the convolutional model exhibits greater resilience and produces higher quality sub-networks compared to the fully connected model, despite ultimately requiring one more phase of pruning to match the accuracy of its pruned counterpart. Our findings also reveal that the surviving neurons in both models exhibit similar inherent characteristics and can be effectively utilized in these models as a form of "intrinsic feature extraction." However, the convolutional model demonstrates an added advantage of being more adept at extracting features at a regional level, which ultimately contributes to its superior performance.

In the realm of online auctions, the value of virtual items lies in their potential outcomes. To secure a valuable outcome, a limited number of bidding rounds must be employed while keeping opponents in the market. A strategy known as THIT was developed to optimize expected gain through repeated bidding. In this study, a modified version of THIT is introduced that aims to maximize the anticipated value of a ticket. To achieve this, a crucial step is added to the process: projected ticket analysis. At each bidding stage, this step involves an option to recycle an existing ticket or acquire a new one. By combining the original THIT mechanism with the new anticipated value optimization method, two hybrid strategies, THIT-Sell and THIT-Buy, are created. Numerical simulations demonstrate the efficacy of the hybrid approach, revealing that THIT-Buy performs better in most market conditions and is more resilient to opponent actions. Additionally, under specific circumstances, THIT-Sell surpasses THIT-Buy, while THIT-Buy consistently dominates when opponents are active in the market.

The value of the critical exponent $\gamma$ for various types of scalar operators $\phi^Q$ with 2 ≤ Q ≤ 5, in the context of O(N) symmetric models, is now known at the six-loop level. This was achieved by building on previously computed information about the related critical exponent γ_{\tau} from the O(N) model with additional dimensions, using a method that involves representing a general spin Q operator in terms of tensors with rank up to five. This allowed us to identify the values of relevant spurious operators at six loops. Previous results from computing the critical exponent γ at four and six loops are also refined. This research enhances our understanding of critical behavior in the O(N) model with five distinct components, specifically in its N = 3 and N = 5 variants. This work is particularly relevant to studying critical behavior in general Q = 5 operators across the N ≥ 5 component range. The results from this research were derived in the framework of the Hamiltonian critical fixed point with a method that involves representing a general spin Q operator in terms of tensors of rank up to five. This allows us to identify the values of related secondary critical exponents at six loops. Our results also reveal that certain operators with rank up to five are equivalent at tree level, Ref.[21]. This work is the basis for a more in-depth investigation of critical behavior in the O(N) model with five distinct components, specifically in its N = 5 variant.

Our research focuses on the effect of new electron-phonon interactions on valley behavior in two-dimensional materials through theoretical analysis and simulation. We find that certain symmetry-allowed polynomial couplings between phonons and valley indices are equivalent to a linear coupling known as the valley Hall coupling. The formation of these couplings is explained by a deformation of the 2D material's circle, resulting in couplings between rotations and valley indices, and we find that this rotation coupling has significant effects on valley Hall effect. Our analytical findings are confirmed through a perturbation theory and transport simulation, and we use this theory to demonstrate that the valley Hall effect can be realized in 2D materials without intrinsic spin-rotation coupling.

The VisDA 2022 Challenge is a data adaptation competition that demands significant skill in handling unseen tasks due to its focus on object-centric domain shifts. In the spirit of the open research initiative, we share our winning strategy with the academic community. Despite an initial assessment suggesting that object-bias was the primary driver of domain disparity, a detailed analysis revealed that this was not the only factor. Within the challenging Simulated Domain Adaptation sub-track of the challenge, our unsupervised adaptation technique outperformed other methods by leveraging the potential of asymmetric training. Our unsupervised adaptation method relies on a dual-loss, asymmetric multi-stage graph neural network architecture that utilizes multi-layer perceptrons. This robust technique is capable of handling a variety of target data distributions by effectively handling the difference in target data classes and densities. Our method's self-supervised approach also helps to mitigate the alignment of unsupervised feature representations and an efficient classifier that handles distribution density disparities. As an open-source contribution, we provide the code on GitHub for the multi-stage GNN, referred to as autoGNN. Our method's unique unsupervised, dense-based training approach successfully adapts to the challenging Simulated Domain Adaptation distribution, an extremely object-centric scenario. Our method also develops an innovative, efficient unsupervised strategy for handling target data densities, referred to as target density aware. Our method's target data density analysis reveals the effective use of an efficient density estimator that predicts the target data density distribution. Our results

t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower dimensions while preserving local similarities, notably in the study of single-cell RNA-seq data. However, its effectiveness is hampered when dealing with data from spheres or highly curved surfaces such as cell surface proteomes, due to the non-uniform nature of the data. By incorporating a prior knowledge of the data's spherical structure, our novel VMF-SNE approach addresses this issue and enhances the quality of its reductions. In comparison to conventional t-SNE, our method yields more accurate reductions of sphere-shaped data, as demonstrated through the analysis of protein sequences. Furthermore, our results reveal that incorporating domain information can reveal distinct clusters within the data.

We apply the coherent state representation in a straightforward manner to formulate the diagrammatic Monte Carlo approach for the Fermi polaron in two dimensions, without relying on assumptions like orthogonality. Our strategy centers on optimizing the variational wave function by including varying numbers of diagrams at each Monte Carlo step. Surprisingly, this method produces results that supplant the theoretical limit and provide a clear pathway for accounting for the effects of higher-order diagrams in the calculations. Our investigation into the observed polaron properties indicates that they are insensitive to the choice of imaginary time at late stages in the evolution. Furthermore, while the polaron size appears to be influenced by the interaction strength, it is largely unaffected by the alignment of the alignment parameter. It's also worth noting that the observed dimer decay rate is primarily attributed to the effects of high-energy quasiparticle excitations, which can be accurately modeled using the weak coupling approximation.

Recent advancements in quantum simulation have yielded substantial outcomes, with notable achievements in both fundamental research and technological applications. This study examines the feasibility of emulating complex fermionic systems using a hybrid digital-analog quantum computing approach and identifies an optimal method for efficiently simulating fermionic behavior. By utilizing a single mode of an optical cavity combined with a superconducting qubit, we successfully obtain the desired fermionic interaction and achieve a high fidelity when simulating the fermionic system. This robust platform enables the simulation of larger fermionic systems, potentially leading to significant advancements in both theoretical research and practical applications.

Graph polynomials hold significant value due to their potential to develop algorithms for degree-counting and exact polynomial equations between various graph invariants. The study of graph polynomials involves analyzing sequences of polynomials associated with graphs, which are called generalised graph polynomials. It provides a class of polynomials that encompasses well-known graph polynomials such as the Chi-polynomial, the Rayleigh polynomial, and the Q-polynomial. The investigation of these generalized polynomials enables a deeper understanding of graph polynomial theory, enabling conclusions to be drawn about specific polynomials. As an example, it is demonstrated that the Chi-polynomial and the Q-polynomial of non-bipartite graphs are irreducible polynomials.

We derive explicit formulas for the moduli space of Veech curves in the genus 3 Veech curve example, involving curves with a $\wp$-family component. Notably, this example's 1-dimensional compactified Veech curve moduli space matches a 1-dimensional component of the 0-dimensional Chow scheme $\chi_{2d}^{1}(\mathbb{P}^1)$, where $d=6$ or $3k^2$ for $k>0$. These formulas for the genus 3 case also address a related Hilbert point problem, and similarly, formulas for the genus 5 case involve a $\wp$-family component. Furthermore, our study indicates that the Chow module $\chi_{2d}(\mathbb{P}^1)$ has a 0-dimensional component representing Hilbert points for a substantial set of $d$ values, exceeding the $2\cdot 60$ values covered by Gurevich and Pazuki's findings. Moreover, our theorems imply that the Chow module $\chi_{2d}(\mathbb{P}^1)$ exhibits a 0-dimensional component for a much larger set of $d$ values of the form $3k^2$ and some exceptional situations. Our analysis also draws connections between the Genus 0 Veech curves and Farkas' findings on the moduli space of Genus 0 curves with a degree multiple

The global COVID-19 pandemic triggered a widespread shift to remote work.
Notably, both researchers and practitioners are still seeking to understand the effects of this transformation in software engineering contexts.
 specifically regarding the success of projects managed using Scrum, a popular framework for managing agile software development projects.
The present study aims to analyze the impact of remote work on Scrum projects' outcomes by examining a diverse sample of 519 professionals from 31 countries.
Our conventional survey approached gathered data on working from home, team collaboration, and Scrum process usage, along with indicators for project success through multi-block partial least squares.
Our investigation reveals that remote work has a positive relationship with project success, despite some limitations.
Moreover, we found successful Scrum practices like daily stand-ups and retrospective increase the beneficial effects of remote work.
Our research also indicates that remote workers face difficulties with poor communication, which may negatively impact project success.
Our study offers insights for practitioners and organizations involved in software development to effectively navigate the challenges and opportunities presented by remote work.

The author of this note independently derived a formula for calculating the Gau-Wu value of a 4x4 matrix, defined as the determinant of a matrix that combines the given matrix with a matrix transformed by a specific rotation, and found that this value must be an even integer. Building on this finding, a general formula for the Gau-Wu value of certain specially constructed matrices, known as arrowhead matrices, is established in terms of specific variables used in their construction. It has been previously established that these variables are interrelated in a way that involves complex number properties, specifically related to the rotation of a vector in a plane, known as the rotaion group of order 2, and a recent study of these elements found that certain combinations must always be even. And so, a formula for the Gau-Wu value, which relies on the determinant of a matrix that combines the given matrix with a matrix transformed by a specific rotation, is established in a way that expresses it in terms of specific variables used in its construction, and the study shows that this value must always be even. And finally, a formula for the Gau-Wu value, which expresses it in terms of specific variables used in its construction, is established in a way that expresses it in terms of specific variables used in its construction.

In this study, the elliptical flow of electrons produced from decays of charm and beauty particles has been investigated in lead-lead collisions at a specific energy level (5.02 TeV). A distinction was established between the collective movement of electrons caused by the early state and the influence of final-state interactions. Using advanced decay simulations, the influence of these processes on the final result was assessed. Accounting for these factors, the average elliptical movement of electrons at a specific range was found to be consistent with theoretical predictions generated using transport models. However, the average elliptical movement of electrons across the entire range was greater than predicted by these models, suggesting the need for further modeling to understand this phenomenon.

In recent years, research on the application of algebraic topology in graph theory has been increasingly popular. Graphs can be represented through topological tools like alpha structures, which allow for the analysis of graph properties using algebraic topology methods. This research introduces the application of persistent homology to the study of graphs. Specifically, we develop techniques to detect features in graphs using persistent homology, focusing on the role of color assignments. By combining the tools of persistent homology with those of homology, we establish criteria for the detection of substructures within graphs based on their coloring. These tools can be utilized in the study of special graph classes, such as planar graphs, and provide a new method for the analysis of graph data.

This work utilizes the concepts from the Generalized DoF (GDoF) analysis to examine the effects of binary power control (BPC) and optimal power control (OPC) in a network with $K$ coexisting users, where each user's transmission is subject to either power constraint. It's shown that while these two methods share many similarities, their performance differs dramatically when attempting to maximize the overall network capacity. Specifically, when focusing on the extreme case, it's proven that OPC outperforms BPC by a factor of at least some non-negative, increasing function of $K$, and at most another such function. Ultimately, these findings provide valuable insights for controlling the level of interference in large-scale networks, where choosing the power transmission levels can significantly impact the efficiency of the network.

Auditing is an intricate process that requires articulation and categorization to prioritize actions effectively. This research develops adaptable categorization techniques based on formal concept analysis and the Dempster-Shafer theory to provide auditing teams with flexible classifications tailored to their objectives. Our method combines these two techniques to tackle both sub-goal and main goal categorization, resulting in adaptive classifications that are more relevant and efficient. Additionally, the approach allows for sub-objectives to be dynamically selected from a broader scope, enhancing its flexibility. A demonstration of this technique is presented, focusing on an adaptable classification of security incident categorization for auditing purposes.

A point process characterized by its use of a pairwise interaction function is called a lattice process, establishing a connection with a differential equation to help in generating such a process randomly. However, many such point processes are difficult to directly simulate because they lack a straightforward relationship with a related partial differential equation. In such cases, a random field can be used as a point process proxy by applying it to the point process, but this often involves solving a non-stationary and backward-looking partial differential equation. In this paper, we introduce a novel technique called "stitching" that uses regular time steps to approximate the solution of this PDE over specific intervals instead. We then utilize this technique to create an efficient method for generating the Strauss point process, making it possible to apply this technique to larger scales such as three-dimensional space.

In the context of string theory and quantum gravity, the generalized uncertainty principle emerges as a key concept that introduces corrections to position and momentum commutators. Building upon this concept, the research incorporates modifications to Lorentz and Galilean transformations to demonstrate how the generalized uncertainty principle affects coordinate and momentum measurements in both relativistic and non-relativistic scenarios.

We consider a Multitasking Allocation Model where multiple agents contribute to multiple tasks, all of which share a common goal. Each agent can choose to contribute to multiple activities, and their individual successes combine logically to achieve collective success. We explore two key decisions: how many tasks each agent should focus on and how successful each agent should be. Current models often simplify which tasks to prioritize by assuming a single task is dominant, or they set a fixed level of effort across all tasks. In contrast, we create a theory that allows multiple tasks to compete for each agent's full effort and calculate optimal efforts for every agent and task. Our framework is versatile and applies to various work environments, including situations where some tasks are more important than others. We demonstrate that our model provides clear and predictable outcomes, and our predictions show a substantial link between an agent's abilities and their available time. Our theory also identifies how to divide time between tasks when some tasks require more effort than others. Additionally, we find that our model's predictions are close to those of a realistic game where all tasks compete for each agent's full effort. Finally, we use our theory to show how an agent's abilities and available time influence their influence on a particular task. Our model calculates these relationships for multiple tasks and our results show a method to divide time between tasks when each task requires a different level of effort. Our findings based on survey data support our theory and provide insights into how an agent's skills and available time relate to their influence and

This research delves into the computational modeling, simulation, and optimization of a one-legged robot capable of hopping as it navigates through yieldable and deformable terrain. The algorithm utilized is predictive feedback linearization paired with a prosthetic root design, enabling the mini-legged robot to apply controlled forces and maintain stability while moving across various surfaces. By merging plant modeling and control strategies into a simultaneous optimization process, different designs can be analyzed with respect to their performance, including their ability to jump, balance, and traverse complex environments efficiently. Various studies have been conducted to examine the impact of distinct parameter configurations. The validity of the developed model was verified through experimental testing and data comparison. This research resulted in several outstanding findings that identified the most effective parameters leading to enhanced movement capabilities.

Integrating firmware updates into IoT devices, now a recommended practice, necessitates thorough evaluation of the impact on mesh networks. This involves assessing performance in terms of network robustness, particularly in situations leading to disconnects and reconnections. Investigating these effects through large-scale networks, we examined not only the mesh network itself, but also the trustworthiness of the resulting network topology post-update, utilizing a mesh network of IoT routers as a model. Our research focused on the practicality of deploying robust and reliable firmware updates in real-world large-scale mesh networks, and we looked at reconnection dynamics following common disconnect events. Ultimately, we identified the primary challenges in deploying updates and suggested potential solutions to enhance firmware update processes.

We explore a novel issue in interactive search, where the objective is to find multiple undistinguishable entities within a totally ordered array using a single mechanism, at a cost not exceeding $k$ where $k$ is the number of entities sought after. We have conducted in-depth analysis on this problem, deriving optimal strategies for various $k$. A key finding shows that for $k$ ranging from $1$ to $5$, a specific strategy is optimal, involving a particular type of binary search. When $k$ equals $6$ or more, and given a cost function of $f(k)$, our results show the optimal strategy involves $O(\frac{\log N}{f(k-1)}}$ queries for a range of $N$, where $N$ represents the total number of items in the array. Additionally, our analysis yields precise asymptotic results for $f(k)$, with a limit of $f(7)$ being undetermined.

Universal adversaries exist that can manipulate quantum classifiers' decisions without being detected, regardless of the specific instance used. Our research explores two types of universal adversaries: instance-specific and based on Hilbert-Schmidt test operators. By experimenting with different training methods for quantum classifiers, such as least-squares classifier and maximum likelihood classifier, we found that LSLS is the most susceptible to these universal adversaries. Furthermore, the hypothesis that MS test operators offer the strongest performance in this context has been supported. Our study also evaluated the effectiveness of different error-reducing methods in minimizing the impact of these universal adversaries. The findings demonstrate that quantum classifiers can be vulnerable to these types of attacks, and this may have implications for developing robust quantum machine learning algorithms in the future.

We examine Steklov eigenvalues in nearly round 2-dimensional domains. Our analysis demonstrates that the Steklov eigenvalues are influenced by a rotationally symmetric potential. Furthermore, we have derived explicit error estimates in terms of the L^2 norm of the first eigenvalue, using a recent perturbation theorem by Rojo Angueira and Wei.

In situations where full event traces cannot be obtained due to limitations such as performance issues or data restrictions, it's necessary to verify conformance based on partial trace segments. We've developed an efficient method to check if a given partial trace follows a predefined process by comparing it to a provided trace that accurately follows the process. Unlike alignments that consider complete traces, our approach focuses on partial traces, constructing two types: infix and postfix alignments. Infix alignments are similar to standard alignments but consider the end of the partial trace, whereas postfix alignments consider the start of the trace. We've established a membership test for the set of correctly formed infix and postfix alignments, as well as a membership test for alignments that can be extended to form a correct combination of both types. This allows us to quickly convert a partial trace that does not conform to a process into an aligned partial trace that can be used to identify the parts that do not conform. Furthermore, we've developed a technique to combine alignments in order to quickly verify the conformance of a partial trace. This technique has a performance complexity of O(z), the length of the alignments, making it more efficient for partial traces.

The task of estimating the power that will be transmitted over each mobile channel in a network is a crucial step in designing and optimizing cellular networks. This process involves modeling radio transmission characteristics based on individual subscriber equipment and their corresponding signal paths. Since this information is typically limited to the network's central node, the power prediction must be adapted to each device's specific environment. This paper utilizes a vast dataset of outdoor mobile devices to develop a novel, efficient approach relying on deep convolutional neural networks that requires minimal relevant data for initialization. The proposed method is primarily targeted at enhancing the efficiency of wireless network planning.

A crucial component in AI, temporal planning, deals with creating strategies to execute within time-based constraints, often represented by transitions and timelines. We've developed a precise definition of temporal planning using a logical framework called NTL, which enables planning within dynamic systems with observable changes over time. Additionally, by employing a formal method known as model checking, we've designed a automated procedure to validate whether a given plan is correct or not. This method relies on planning algorithms that produce optimal and feasible solutions, which we then use to create a formal representation of the plan. Our approach has been tested on a well-known planning problem with time-based constraints, demonstrating the effectiveness of our technique.

As countries accelerate their transition to renewable energy, the need to predict and manage energy system changes grows. Origin, DNV GL, and others have developed models for this purpose, such as the Origin Pathway Model or DNV GL's Power System Modeling Platform (PSMP). However, the accuracy and reliability of these models depend heavily on settings for key variables. The process of optimizing model settings, adapting them to new scenarios, and ensuring high data quality is poorly understood and often overlooked. The purpose of this research is to develop a standardized approach for preparing and setting parameters for origin-type power system models, including models from DNV GL and Origin. The study will investigate model run behavior using a common dataset and provide best practices for utilizing and modifying models. The research will also create a tool to assist in defining original parameters and facilitate the sharing of knowledge among model users. The results of this research will significantly improve the accuracy and reliability of power system models and support decision-making for low-carbon investment choices.

We establish global existence for a Vlasov-Poisson-like system within a confined space, consisting of a linear transport equation and its associated Neumann problem. The key condition for our proof is a certain Lipschitz requirement on the interaction term of the system, except for the specific case where this term is constant, in which case we establish a more precise estimate for the associated flow.

When conducting software maintenance, developers typically receive numerous, loosely written requests for change, described in terms of everyday language. In software engineering, the task of pinpointing the specific section that corresponds to a particular change request is denoted as Concept Location. Most existing techniques for Concept Location rely on natural language processing and ask the user to input a query based on the change request, which is then compared with the system's language model. Due to the informal nature of these requests, determining the relevant search terms can be challenging. Existing methods for identifying relevant terms typically rely on domain expertise or prior knowledge, leading to difficulties in applying them to new contexts. In our current study, we presented a novel approach, known as STRICT, for identifying relevant terms using natural language techniques. We treated the change requests, along with a corresponding reference system texts, as a typical information retrieval problem and calculated the relevance of each term using an advanced algorithm. Our results indicate that this approach performs comparably to the best available methods for relevant term identification.

Researchers have discovered a novel approach to modify the mechanical properties of colloidal gels by introducing ultrasonic vibrations. They investigated how these vibrations affect the gel's response to external forces, such as compression, using various techniques, including acoustic measurement and rheometry. The results show that ultrasonic waves can either improve or impair the gel's ability to withstand external forces, depending on its pre-existing structural state. Moreover, these vibrations can significantly reduce the gel's threshold for flow when subjected to a constant stress, while also shifting the onset of flow to higher frequencies. The changes brought on by ultrasonic waves were found to persist even after vibration cessation and resulted in gels with enhanced rigidity. The findings suggest that ultrasonic waves can reorganize the internal structure of colloidal gels, leading to the observed mechanical alterations.

The Collatz Conjecture is a theory in the field of number theory that holds that the Orr Algorithm will produce a sequence leading to the number 1, specifically for any positive integer n. If n is even, the sequence begins with n divided by 2, and if n is odd, it starts with n divided by 3 and plus 1. Notably, the renowned mathematician John Horton Conway described the Orr Algorithm as the "fairest" method in solving the Collatz problem, and this theory is currently undergoing validation for all positive integers.

To effectively organize and make STEM documents easily accessible through search, a precise categorization system is necessary. However, the typical approach to classification proves insufficient for STEM papers as they frequently cover multiple disciplinary areas, requiring either a lengthier classification process or a more complex model to accommodate their complexity. One promising method to improve classification on STEM papers involves extracting key entities from the texts and linking them to relevant subjects in a knowledge graph. By doing so, both specialized and general topics can be identified, allowing for more accurate document categorization. Although Linking Entities, a method developed for natural language texts, can also be applied to STEM documents, the limited presence of entities specific to STEM fields makes it difficult to achieve satisfactory classification results. To address this issue, we have developed Mathematical Entity Linking (MEL), a refined version of Linking Entities designed to work effectively with STEM texts. By incorporating mathematical text analysis and dependency parsing to locate essential entities in STEM documents, MEL is capable of improving classification by as much as 8% in combination with Linking Entities.

We explore a variant of the classic stable marriage problem by focusing on a particular instant in time. In this setting, a set of women with distinct preferences and a set of suitors each choose a potential match. Each individual then selects and "proposes" to the preferred match. Following this, every woman matches with the man to whom she initially proposed, except in cases where they would be better off with a different match. This final arrangement, which we call "final matches," is proven to be stable by demonstrating that any arrangement resulting in a better match for one person must also be a better match for their counterpart. The concept is further expanded to identify the most desirable initial matches, which are defined as "optimal proposals." By applying a particular algorithm that prioritizes matches with the highest rank and using them as few times as possible, we can establish that these proposals are indeed the best and also exist, thereby showing that "optimal proposals" are equivalent to "optimal matchings." We extend this finding to demonstrate that finding these optimal matches is computationally challenging. Additionally, we investigate a scenario in which women can choose not only a particular man but also whether or not to be serious about the match, introducing the concept of seriousnessexpectations.
