This paper provides a counterpoint to a previous study that proposed a universal framework for pricing Asian options. The author notes that while this framework is mathematically accurate, it is not practical for use in industry due to complications resulting from the combination of geometric pricing and dynamic hedging. The paper then presents an alternative method for handling geometric pricing and discusses the implications of using a universal framework for pricing Asian options.

We have used data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope (FERMI-LAT) to measure and analyze the gamma-ray intensity from a sample of galaxy clusters. Our findings suggest that galaxy clusters contribute significantly to gamma-ray intensity, accounting for approximately 15% of the total observed flux above 1 GeV within a 2 pi steradian radius. This percentage increases to around 25% when considering gamma-rays above 10 GeV. Our data show that galaxy clusters follow the same gamma-ray luminosity relationship as the FERMI-LAT observed sources, with a power-law index of 2.33. The primary gamma-ray emission mechanism in galaxy clusters involves the interaction of cosmic rays with the thermal plasma's Alfvén waves. Although the emission varies among the observed galaxy clusters, our data show a consistent pattern across this phenomenon. Our analysis assumes that the observed gamma-ray intensity from galaxy clusters is uniform and consistent across space, an assumption that is validated through the analysis of two methods. Our research further indicates that galaxy clusters serve as a reliable reference point or benchmark to study the gamma-ray intensity and its distribution within the local universe.

We're exploring an cosmological collision event that occurs when space-time is contracting, and two massive objects, mirror images of each other in the universe's center, collide at the Big Crunch or a similar point. Our analysis shows that as these objects, which are fundamental fields embedded in a fiducian universe, move towards each other in space-time, they'll encounter an energy density that is inversely proportional to the power of n for a specific range of n, where n is greater than 4, and then suddenly increase as they collide and enter a region of normal space-time. Our findings indicate that any distinct patterns introduced during this cosmic collision will be smoothed out if these patterns have a specific frequency higher than a certain threshold, and the threshold is directly related to the objects' initial size. Cross-checking our results against simulations from Quantum Field Theory, and also examining what implications our work has on theories known as theories of modified gravity, these simulations confirm our hypothesis, and our work has significant relevance to theories that were initially unmodified.

Understanding how visual recognition models work is essential, and to achieve this goal, researchers have created explanatory techniques. These methods, such as backpropagation-based visual attention, help identify the most relevant visual features used by a model. Nevertheless, these methods are still tied to the specific architecture of a particular model and require adjustments when evaluating other models. In contrast, we present an explanatory method that is inherently applicable to all deep convolutional neural networks, independent of their ResNet variations or other specific implementations. Our novel approach captures the most relevant visual features and corresponding semantic information in a common space, enabling us to visualize the focus of each model filter on specific image regions. Using our method, we demonstrate that models with varying levels of complexity can indeed be effectively explained. Our research encompasses explanations for object recognition in animals and humans, scene understanding in animals and humans, and object categorization in humans, all utilizing the proposed Latent Visual-Semantic Filter Focus method.

The electronic properties of the cuprate family are influenced by a complex combination of factors driven by electron-phonon interactions that lead to subtle changes in the lattice structure. Focusing on one-dimensional cuprates and their lattice distortion similar to that of the self-doped state in infinite-layer compounds, our research explores how this distortion affects electronic transport. Using the tight-binding model, we analyze the transport properties by considering the impact of both first-order (symmetric) and second-order (anti-symmetric) phonon interactions. Consequently, our studies demonstrate the existence of an attractive long-range interaction mediated by phonons and also observe the emergence of a non-monotonic conductivity profile as a result of the first-order phonon interaction. Ultimately, our work aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of the phonon role in determining electronic characteristics in cuprate materials.

Non-Experimental Small Sample Relational Machine Learning Domain Literature suggests that discovering the causal structure of data generated by observational experiments faces significant challenges due to diverse data sources, numerous hidden variables, and diverse underlying causal structures. This study addresses these challenges by developing an innovative approach to uncover the causal structure present in the Australian Medical Health dataset, which consists of genetic and medical information related to an individual's health. This personal data is usually stored in multiple databases linked through unique identifiers. Existing data mining techniques have ignored the discovery of causal structures in this context, instead directly exploring specific relationships. Our work innovates by uncovering the hidden patterns in this data, successfully distinguishing between individual and population health, while demonstrating that individual health is primarily determined by genetics. Additionally, our research uses conditional mutual information to eliminate incorrect causal structures, resulting in an efficient algorithm with improved performance. Our results significantly surpass the state-of-the-art in uncovering the causal structure present in health datasets.

Investigations into the Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ magnet, known for its stability and magnetic properties when near its phase transition, provide valuable insights into the dynamics of magnetic patterns. Specifically, it exhibits robustness against the traditional forces that influence magnetic pattern collapse. Notably, it exhibits a unique phase transition that cannot be explained by the standard theory of pattern formation. Instead, it suggests a transition from one type of magnetic arrangement to another. Our experiments and simulations demonstrate that the sudden change in the arrangement of magnetic spires within the pattern, known as a skyrmion lattice, is a result of the sudden loss of stability of the original lattice. This loss of stability, known as unstable topological melting, is a unique phenomenon that has not been seen before. For certain parameters, it even exists at temperatures where the material is still in a state of magnetic inhomogeneity. The material's properties can be manipulated to observe different arrangements of magnetic spires within the pattern, including arrangements within the pattern and the pattern itself. The ability to control the arrangements of magnetic spires within the pattern, known as "chiral domains", is a result of adjusting the material's electron structure. The discovery of unstable topological melting and its distinct features could influence the understanding of similar phenomena in similar systems, potentially occurring in other types of magnets.

High-dimensional data analysis in economics, finance, and related disciplines often employs statistical and statistical-learning methods to build complex models. These models, which typically consist of small parameter sets relative to a large number of non-parametric components, rely on limited information and seek to leverage additional assumptions, constraints, and data. This overview outlines various types of high-dimensional models, highlighting key model specification, performance constraints, distinct methods, significant results, and significant challenges, as well as forecasting future areas of investigation.

This paper investigates the fixed-point technique for solving equilibrium problems under specific conditions. To achieve this, an equilibrium problem is first mapped onto a nonlinear optimization issue using a mixed-integer support function approximation method. Subsequently, fixed-point iterations utilizing Minty's variant are applied to solve the optimization problem, yielding the desired solution. An extensive numerical example demonstrates the utility of this approach for solving a nonlinear optimal control problem. However, it should be noted that in the vast majority of instances, fixed-point iterations will fail to converge due to discretization errors, rendering this method largely impractical for general use.

In previous research, an open-source framework was developed for making adaptive image forgery detection systems more practical and affordable to deploy. Here, we focus on the reverse process - an innovative method of creating forged images that can evade detection by existing systems without revealing their inner workings. Our technique involves generating forged images from given text prompts using a reversible concealment approach. An elaborate generative model was designed to produce artifact-free output. However, the complexity of the model, along with the limited availability of data, poses significant challenges to training the model's parameters reliably. To overcome this problem, a Bayesian Neural Network was employed as the generative model, allowing us to derive a computationally efficient approximation of the full posterior distribution. Our results indicate that images forged using this method are nearly undistinguishable from real images and can successfully evade the detection of widely-trained classifiers without revealing the architecture of the forgery model.

The use of mean-field hydrodynamic and magnetohydrodynamic models has shown promise in understanding complex, large-scale solar and stellar dynamics by relating small-scale turbulence to its effects on rotation and magnetic field behavior. To create an accurate representation of these processes, the effect of turbulence needs to be fully characterized through determination of all related differential operators beyond previously computed second-order derivatives. To obtain a complete spectrum, especially the fourth-order operator, numerical methods must be employed given the current state of theoretical knowledge. In our study, we use a global spherical harmonics representation to simulate convection in stars and the Earth by modeling its initial energy distribution and relevant physical parameters. By incorporating turbulent effects as operator mappings rather than empirical formulas, the simulated geophysical and astrophysical dynamics are significantly influenced. In particular, our findings reveal the necessity of including higher-order operators beyond the standard alpha-effect operator to accurately describe long-term dynamics and radial differential rotation in the Sun, the other stars, and the Earth. In conclusion, the developed global numerical approach allows for an in-depth exploration of various dynamo types, including the alpha-effect dynamo, mean-field induction dynamo, and diffusion dynamo, which are powered by turbulent effects in global, differentially rotating, and uniformly magnetized objects.

The powerful jet-like outflows seen in the centers of many Galaxies are believed to be driven by the power of Supermassive Black Holes. Recent discoveries made using molecular line observations have revealed these outflows not just confined to the outer regions of galaxies but also existing close to their cores. Using a powerful ALMA instrument, the team was able to detect and study the molecular gas from the center of NGC4945 for the first time. The data showed that this molecular gas has an speed of at least 1200 km per second, has a narrow distribution, and has formed a structure resembling a complete ring around 16 parsecs in diameter. The efficiency with which it has been ejected is very high with an estimated rate of which can transport a massive gas with the mass of our own Sun within just a few years. The data suggests that it is the highly energetic and rotational energy of the Supermassive Black Hole that is driving this ejection. The ejection process is highly efficient here as unlike in most cases where it is driven by the outflow from a disk this highly radial ejection occurs within the very center of the disk itself. The data suggests a highly massive nature of the Supermassive Black Hole in NGC4945 with an estimated mass to be in the range of 1.5 to 9 million times that of our own Sun. The data suggests that it is continuously active with its spinal cord like structure constantly being spun at nearly 1000 revolutions per minute.

A simplified mathematical framework, known as quasilinear diffusion, has been developed to analyze electron heating processes in space plasmas observed through instruments such as XMM-Newton and OSO-7. This framework is based on a nonlinear interaction model between the plasma density fluctuations and the underlying magnetic field. A novel implicit solver for the kinetic equation has been created using a variational approach, resulting in an efficient numerical solution. This paper presents the development of a conservative numerical scheme for the quasilinear diffusion framework using the Galerkin method, which maintains the accuracy and stability of the discrete system. The method's convergence and stability are analyzed, and several numerical experiments are performed to demonstrate its effectiveness in approximating solutions to the original partial differential equation.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving real-world problems.
We provide a condition for the exponential stability of a c0-semigroup in a Banach space, drawing on the Lyapunov equation.

This paper introduces MuMuPy, a computational software and Python library for predicting how muonium (an exotic atom consisting of a muon and an electron) reacts chemically with substances. It simulates the behavior of muonium in response to the electrostatic forces from the atoms in a substance, allowing it to calculate important properties such as the probability of formation. MuMuPy can be used to determine if it is feasible to create dimuonium compounds, which could serve as a precursor for making them directly. Additionally, the program allows users to generate three-dimensional visualizations of the interaction and calculate the relevant wave functions. A comprehensive user guide is provided to facilitate access to the software and its documentation.

Portfolio management strategies that incorporate two assets, one growing rapidly and the other providing stable growth, are examined in this research. The manager's asset allocation decisions are based on two metrics: the performance of each asset in absolute terms and their comparative performance relative to a market benchmark. The manager's goal is to maximize portfolio returns under a specific utility function that accounts for the risks involved. The utility function used in this study is unique, taking into consideration not only the portfolio's performance but also the comparison between the two assets in relation to the benchmark. The model is then analyzed using mathematical techniques to understand how the manager's decisions are influenced by the proportions of assets allocated and the benchmark. The research also finds a connection between the optimal strategy and a specific mathematical function. The effectiveness of the optimal strategy and its ability to be adapted to various risk levels are demonstrated through numerical examples.

The nature of galactic "dark matter" remains unclear and contributes significantly to galactic physics. Using the most up-to-date kinematic data from 25 dwarf galaxy componenents, we have tested current galactic rotation curve models and further examined the relationship between galactic weight and light. We have found strong evidence for dark matter in 20 of these components and, although some data supports the galactic "dark matter" hypothesis, the inconsistent results among individual galaxies pose certain challenges to the theory. Furthermore, we have discovered that the mass-to-light ratios of dark matter, as determined from rotation curves, are consistent across all dwarf galaxy components. This finding has been replicated, however it remains that the underlying explanation for the observed patterns in the universe remains unknown. Finally, we have compiled new IGM flow cylinder velocity data for 25 dwarf galaxy components and found that the velocity of dark matter, as measured, does not change significantly with the mass of the galaxy.

We've discovered an unexpected consequence of interacting with local oscillations, specifically in systems where the presence of these oscillations affects the mass of the particles involved. In our theoretical model, we see that when the oscillations are strong enough, they cause a unique type of phase transition where the distinct components of the system disappear and form a more uniform state. In our investigation, we focused on how this oscillations affect the critical point of this phase transition and were surprised to find that this system cannot be adequately described using existing simple models. To effectively describe this system, we had to consider the complex interactions among the different components involved. We were able to demonstrate that this complex interaction is the result of the distinct components involved surviving as distinct components even in the presence of these oscillations. In a second part of our investigation, we were able to demonstrate that this new method for describing this system is the result of a unique type of relationship between the distinct components involved and their interactions. This new relationship is responsible for the distinct components involved surviving as distinct components even in the presence of these oscillations.

The primary objective of this research is to investigate the divergence properties for a broad range of group mappings, including the generalised Thompson groups, their Thompson group counterparts, braided groups, and braided-Thompson groups. Specifically, we will demonstrate that $G$ is a divergence group, $G \times G$ exhibits uniform divergence, and the natural two-variable function mapping associated with $G$ has local uniform divergence. Notably, our findings yield new insights for the Thompson group $F$, particularly the local uniform divergence property, whereas we establish the divergence property for $F$ without relying on prior work, including bucks and cohomology methods. Furthermore, our analysis extends the divergence characteristics to the braided group $(F, \sigma)$, particularly its generalised Thompson group equivalents, and the effective computation of certain weighted summations involving the Thompson group mapping.

This paper will explore the process of refining the Complete RAG model for question-answering tasks. Initially, we'll examine how it works in conjunction with the DPR retriever. Subsequently, we'll document our efforts to optimize it for the WikiQA 8b dataset, eventually drawing connections to recent advancements in large language models.

This paper calculates the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients for polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to a specific weight function, known as the logarithmic influence, given by $\e^{-2Q}$ where $Q$ is a convex function, within a specific interval. The calculations rely on the connection between these coefficients and the solutions of a non-linear differential equation, known as the second Painlev\'e equation. The solutions to this equation, known to be unbounded as $x$ approaches its boundary, pose an obstacle to the orthogonality conditions which demand the solutions remain bounded. This paradox is resolved by considering an appropriate modification to the weight function, resulting in a new limit behavior distinct from that of the original as $x$ approaches its boundary.

Crowdsourcing has proven effective in gathering diverse opinions on various topics, yet the process often faces challenges when targeting specific, low-volume groups. Research on MTurk crowdsourcing indicates that only 1 in 5 workers without a US degree or in a low education level has shared their demographic information, and even among those who have, many hide their actual qualifications by manipulating their profile or hiding their previous work history. We found that when we looked at worker education, about 60% of the workers with unverified demographics matched the expected education based on their profile. We speculate that many workers with verified demographics are truthful, but the number of unverified demographically qualified workers remains hidden. In contrast, when we analyzed workers without a college degree, we only got 16 more, indicating that the pool of unverified workers is extremely small. We speculate that workers without a college degree are less likely to hide their demographic information. We discovered that when we narrowed the search for workers without a college degree to those with specific job histories, we were able to get 25, and later 49 more, increasing the sample size to 105. We speculate that workers without a college degree are more likely to hide their demographic information as they get older in their career. Short video recordings, known as text-clips, are becoming increasingly significant on a variety of applications including video analysis, content creation and search functions. In this context, a novel retrieval task referred to as text-clips retrieval has emerged which necessitates the design of a system capable of effectively matching the underlying text content within these short videos with long-form text-based descriptions. Existing text-based retrieval methods used so far have proven to be insufficient for achieving optimal results in this specific task. In our research paper, a traditional transformer's limitations in text-clips retrieval are addressed through the creation of a novel network called TS2-Net, an improved transformer-based solution. TS2-Net involves token shift and selection processes that make use of attention-based techniques. By implementing these processes, a reduced yet significant subset of tokens is selected and re-ordered from the input text-clips prior to matching operations, allowing for a concurrent consideration of both the visual and textual aspects within these recordings. Our research includes a comprehensive understanding of text-clips retrieval including a newly introduced dataset known as TVRetreat, comprising 20,000 video-clips coupled with relevant text-based descriptions and indicators of ranking importance. Our findings demonstrate that the TS2-Net approach significantly surpasses all other existing retrieval techniques in terms of both the accuracy of matching and the overall search performance. Our research findings as well as the newly developed dataset are made publicly accessible to the research community.

The concept of taste-changing neutral currents is an interesting extension of the flavor sector of the Standard Model, with topological effects that differ from those in the lepton and light quark flavor sectors. This report outlines a theory on neutral currents with topological characteristics beyond those in the established model, where such currents beyond the established model, if detected, could provide a clear indication of new physics. Additionally, it is explained how such neutral currents beyond the established model can influence CP violation effects in various processes, leading to observable implications in specific contexts, such as in the decay of heavy quarks and in particle collisions at current or future facilities.

A new class of directed hybrid random graphs has been introduced, which combine features of directed preference and uniform attachment mechanisms to model real-world complex interactions. These hybrid models subsume both uniform attachment directed graphs and supercritical directed preferential attachment models, which are widely used in theory and applications, as special cases. Our study provides a comprehensive analysis of directed hybrid random graphs, including calculations for key properties like the degree distribution, clustering coefficients, and out-degree and in-degree distributions. Additionally, our investigation into the evolution of the graph structure from an initial state to a steady-state configuration, along with a comparison of its mixing time, degree distribution, and clustering coefficients with those of large-scale information networks, offers valuable insights into their developing behavior. Our main contribution lies in the rigorous mathematical proof of a stationary state that emerges in the growing hybrid graph, supported by numerical simulations and case studies, which further validate our theoretical findings.

The fast-lensing expansion of wireless services necessitates ensuring minimal interference to existing systems as new networks are deployed. Interference can be easily overlooked in frequency planning for new wireless systems, which might ultimately result in suboptimal performance and data losses. Therefore, accurately pinpointing interference causes is essential for effective problem diagnosis and data-driven strategy development. With the impending release of 6 GHz bandwidths and the gradual integration of AI into wireless technology, along with a shift towards universal wireless access, diagnosing interference will increasingly involve AI techniques. However, existing methods for detecting disturbance types are limited and typically address a single disturbance at a time. In our proposed work, we introduce a novel framework for identifying multiple disturbance types simultaneously. This framework leverages convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to analyze spatial channel correlations and predict disturbance locations. Our findings based on extensive simulations indicate that the proposed approach outperforms current metrics in identifying multiple disturbance types. Our research marks the first application of CNNs in wireless disturbance identification and lays the groundwork for using machine learning in wireless system development.

This research examines the interactions of spinless particles represented by Klein-Gordon equations within a cosmic string spacetime contaminated by space-time defects. The effective potential, appearing in the Klein-Gordon focus, manifests as a combination of a cosmic string spacetime's intrinsic potential and defects' potential resulting from location disparities. The study initially solves the Klein-Gordon equation for its solution and relevant constant $k$, assuming a particle's initial quantum state, when a defect is absent. Subsequently, it expresses the solution and $k$ in terms of a defect parameter $\epsilon$. Using quantum conditions, the study determines the particle's initial quantum state along a defect-free cosmic string spacetime, for various $\epsilon$ values. Additionally, it illustrates the localization of the solution through a symmetries-based approach. Furthermore, it computes the conjugate momentum, quantum vorticity, and energy in a defect-free cosmic string spacetime, for different $\epsilon$ values. The study reveals that the effects of a cosmic string spacetime and its defects on conjugate momentum, quantum vorticity, and energy are interdependent.

In the context of nonlocal analysis, our subject of investigation centers around
measure spaces with a countable base that adhere to a specific condition. Specifically,
within such spaces, a measure algebra is introduced, characterized by the selection
of a Borel-measurable subset of non-negative measures that assigns a constant
value to measurable sets of identical measure. It's demonstrated that these measure algebras
behave much like their localized counterparts in standard model. Moreover, a certain
uniqueness property holds for the primary measure within each class.

Dynamical Vertical Cuts (DVCS) separates into electron perturbation and hadron reaction contributions after integration, with the latter involving a single scale, unlike electron perturbation which involves a range of scales.  A new observable, involving the polarization of the recoiled proton, has been proposed which due to its Hadron Mass dependence, wouldn't be found with traditional general QCD frameworks, thus allowing the separation of DVCS contributions at a kinematic level not previously achievable with leading twist methods.

The development of synthetic intelligent entities is advancing rapidly in both their design and functionality. As a consequence, multiple forms of synthetic intelligence have emerged, influenced by distinct viewpoints and objectives. A fundamental challenge arises from the lack of a unified theoretical approach, leading to diverse definitions and understanding of synthetic intelligence. In response to this gap, we propose a conceptual framework for augmented synthetic intelligence, dividing it into two categories: 'augmented' referring to the integration of multiple forms of intelligence, and'synthetic' signifying the creation of novel, artificial intelligence through data-driven and resource-based construction. By establishing a solid foundation for augmented synthetic intelligence, we can further develop its underlying principles and design principles, ultimately enabling the design and development of innovative synthetic intelligent entities.

Our research involves exploring the thermal behavior of the Bose-Hubbard model for indistinguishable bosons with spin-orbit linked correlations, which exhibit an underlying superfluid with various quantum states. Due to strong spin-orbit coupling, these states become intertwined, ultimately resulting in a non-Abelian topological phase demonstration. Contrary to expectations, when the system undergoes a phase transition at finite temperatures, rather than losing its long-range order, it develops a complex mixture of several non-topological states that persists across all temperatures. However, at very low temperatures, the system undergoes an unconventional phase transition and enters a topological state characterized by complex entanglement. Our research involves a novel approach using an extended Hubbard model and quantum Monte Carlo simulations to model this process.

A real linear transformation of an n-dimensional vector space defines a graph by linking pairs of vectors that transform into each other under the given mapping. This paper examines all such graphs and their variations. It demonstrates how different types of these graphs, by their degree, symmetry, and form, are classified. Specifically, it shows that the existing graphs of a certain class can degenerate into the earlier forms as the dimension increases. Furthermore, it proves that every graph of this nature can be expressed as the combination of identical, identical rotational versions of a certain defined graph. This study also yields consequences in another related area: the structure of certain groups' orbits within a specific mathematical space.

Recent breakthroughs in AdS/CFT correspondence research, specifically in low-dimensional settings, are explored through an alternative approach in type IIA AdS black holes with transverse space complexity. This occurs above a specific critical positive scalar mass threshold in the dual field theory, where a particular spin type experiences mass dependence in a nonlinear manner. Notably, for four-dimensional cases, a phase transition involving condensation is observed, associated with a first-order phase transition in the AdS black hole's temperature, while in three-dimensional settings, a novel instability in the holographic dual translates to a similar condensation-induced phase transition, where the field's energy density is directly proportional to the critical temperature difference. This distinct physics stems from a particular spin type in type IIA AdS black holes with non-zero dilaton, which was previously unexplored. Furthermore, specific examples incorporating global symmetry violations and deformations into two-dimensional conformal theories are provided, involving a sine-Lattice model and a free fermion theory. These examples, in conjunction with their holographic instabilities, reveal previously unknown properties in their respective field theories, incorporating aspects of condensation and chiral symmetry breaking.

The applications of Gaussian Process regression have shown significant utility due to its ability to construct informative probabilistic models from limited data. The success of GP models heavily relies on the choice of an appropriate kernel function. In the past, these functions were derived using complex mathematical derivations and approximations. This work aims to establish a method for developing GP kernels using a straightforward and structured approach based on fundamental mathematical expressions. The methodology involves systematically generating a space of GP models by applying a given set of kernels to different variables, enabling an exhaustive exploration of the associated conditionality properties. This paper demonstrates the method with two kernel types derived using elementary vector representations, which form the basis of a proposed Gaussian Process framework called Symbolic Kernel Development for Dynamic Estimation (SKDDE). The SKDDE framework is distinguished by its explicit and predictable behavior, allowing for a manageable search of conditionality properties within practical bounds. Additionally, the framework provides an understandable symbolic representation of GP models, making it easily interpretable. The method has been tested and validated on a 10DOF vehicle system. The findings show that there are sufficient kernel options that can meet the requirements for this specific application, all of which were identified through a computationally feasible search. The research further analyzes the trade-offs in the chosen kernels, emphasizing their practical implications in advanced control applications.

Future muon colliders will likely be constructed in the form of a straight line
circle, generating a substantial number of muons at each segment which is then
circulated to produce the desired collision results. However, the process of
producing these muons also gives rise to a type of background radiation known as
beam-induced noise, which poses a significant threat to achieving sufficient
signal resolution for these colliders. In this research, we have identified and
evaluated several methods aimed at minimizing beam-induced noise through the
analysis of ionization, capture, and utilization of natural radioactive isotopes.
Our findings suggest that the main sources of background radiation can be controlled
by employing suitable methods to regulate the formation of these muons at
optimized rates, utilizing an appropriate mixture of radioactive isotopes to
produce the initial muons, and increasing the lifespan of muon particles in the
circulated circle to counteract decay-related background radiation. Additionally,
our research has identified several areas where further study or enhancement is
required to support these strategies and support the overall design and construction
of future muon colliders, including the optimization of muon production rates,
the identification and management of radioactive isotopes to minimize excessive
components, the improvement of circular muon lifespan through the optimization of
the utilization of radioactive isotopes, the development of more precise simulation
models for accurate prediction and simulation of background radiation, and the
evaluation of circled muon states to accurately predict their natural

We introduce a new method to impose sparsity in neural networks in a differentiable manner, which can be used with various loss functions. This method consists of three components: 1) a regularized transportation constraint that includes all possible assignments of inputs to outputs and ensures complete utilization of inputs, 2) a constrained weighted average operation that acts as a differentiable alternative to selective forwarding of inputs, and 3) a dual regularization technique that induces sparsity in the output of a neural network. This method is then used to develop a differentiable priority encoder, which is used in various applications such as visual search, policy evaluation, and reinforcement learning. This method is viewed as a novel approach to implementing a global "attention" mechanism in neural networks.

In three-dimensional Bose gases with weak interactions, an emergent phenomenon
arises from the formation of virtual bound states at the intersection of single-particle
waves. A supplementary contribution to the Pauli obstruction is provided by these
bound states, via a derived expression for the Pauli obstruction in terms of the scattering
length and system parameters. Although the bound states disappear in the continuum
limit, our findings show that they leave behind a non-deleted topological characteristic
involving the Hessian of the effective Hamiltonian.

Software developers widely utilize unit tests to make sure new additions function correctly and fix existing issues. Yet, research has shown that even well-designed tests can fail to catch errors, while poorly constructed tests may hinder the developers' ability to identify and resolve problems. In the software development process, 'test smells' emerge as indicators of poor test quality, potentially hindering developers' productivity and leaving several crucial questions unanswered: What specific test issues do developers view as most critical? Are there any correlations between developers' perspectives and their professional experience? Do their opinions align with established findings from the literature? A survey of Java developers, examining their responses to various types of test smells, has provided new insights, in addition to insights on how experience influences one's ability to identify and interpret test smells.

This study examines a nonconvex version of Schurle's brushing process, an energy-driven model characterized by its distinctive, shell-like, integral-based interactions. The model in question is part of a broader category of gradient systems involving complex, integer-based energy relationships. The ultimate goal is to better understand these models, and to this end, we've demonstrated the model's convergence, mapped its dynamic behavior, and identified key characteristics, including the model reaching a steady state composed of multiple distinct, coexisting phases. Additionally, we've also explored various qualitative properties, such as stability and the model's capacity to exhibit intricate, shell-like patterns that are often absent in simpler models. The findings presented here serve as a crucial stepping stone for interpreting real-world data that can be driven by multiple distinct processes.

We introduce the updated version of {\tt KKMCee}, a Monte Carlo event generator for pair production in electron-positron colliders. In this updated version, we incorporate new features: the ability to simulate not just pair production, but also single-lepton production, as well as quark and antiquark production; integration with {\tt PAI}, a Monte Carlo path simulator, allowing for more accurate simulation of lepton flavors; and, crucially, the incorporation of electron positron pair weak decay processes via {\tt KKMC7}, allowing for decay mechanisms beyond the Yukawa model. We provide example events generated by {\tt KKMCee} for two benchmark scenarios: a 100 TeV $e^+e^-$ center-of-mass energy with neutralino pair production in the CMSSM parameter space at low mass scales, and for W boson pair production at the proposed Higgs factory $e^+e^-$ colliders. These example events are then used to illustrate the feasibility of identifying neutralinos and distinguishing between up and down quarks at future $e^+e^-$ colliders. We show that, for very small mass scales, the equivalent-bracket method is the most effective strategy to identify neutralinos; for up and down quarks, the standard method of forming R-ratios is the most effective strategy. Estimating inter beat intervals from ECG signals can provide valuable insights into heart health. This analysis is crucial for diagnosing various health issues, including cardiovascular diseases. In areas with limited resources, ECG signal processing is also important for interpreting inter beat intervals, which is essential for identifying patients who require immediate medical attention due to life threatening conditions such as arrhythmias, leading to heart failure and sudden cardiac death. The sudden onset of life threatening electrical disorders can only be identified by analyzing inter beat intervals, which in turn enables the identification of heart-related emergencies. This research proposes a novel, Tiramisu-based approach to estimate inter beat intervals from ECG signals. The findings indicate that our estimated inter beat intervals are highly accurate, with a low mean absolute error of 2.06 milliseconds across all 168 segments of the INCART dataset. Furthermore, the estimated inter beat intervals exhibit strong consistency, with a median error ranging from 1 to 9 milliseconds across all segments of the INCART dataset. The estimated inter beat intervals are also significant at the 95% confidence level. Notably, the proposed Tiramisu model has numerous applications in the development of patient-specific models, the identification of disease biomarkers, the development of device-free systems, the design of heart-related image reconstruction techniques, the estimation of heart beats with missing or incomplete data, and the creation of autonomous systems for inter beat estimation and heart health monitoring.

To compute the tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) in an efficient manner, we have developed a new randomized algorithm that can execute the necessary matrix multiplication required for the first step of the decomposition with just a few passes through a large tensor, thereby assessing the feasibility of applying certain data reduction techniques more effectively than before. Assessing the effectiveness with real-world datasets reveals that our method is that of the best-known approaches given a set amount of resources (i.e. matrix multiplications). We have also analyzed the theoretical resources (e.g. statistical complexity) needed for various methods to compute the t-SVD. Our results show that certain decomposition techniques are more efficient than others given a set number of resources (matrix multiplications). We have applied this method to two tensor decomposition techniques: tensor nonnegative orthogonal decompositions and tensor unifying complementarity decompositions. We have also adapted this method to the sparse problem and proved that our method is the most efficient given a set number of resources (matrix multiplications). We have applied this method to two sparse tensor decomposition techniques: tensor nonnegative orthogonal decompositions and tensor complementary decompositions. We have also proven that our method is scalable in terms of a tensor's order (n x n x n) and computed an optimal number of passes (approximately n^2) for the algorithm based on a set number of resources (matrix multiplications).

Real-world networks frequently undergo dynamic changes and evolution. Several crucial applications rely on processing and analyzing these changing graphs, yet their fluid structure presents an analysis difficulty. By embedding these graphs into vector representations of nodes that preserve essential network characteristics, researchers have overcome some challenges associated with analyzing these complex systems. This paper focuses on embedding evolving graphs, defining evolution broadly as changes in their structures over time. It comprehensively surveys existing graph embedding techniques from various viewpoints, categorizing them based on origins and discussions of the implications of evolution, network characteristics, and embedding applications and theories. Furthermore, we highlight the demands and constraints of embedding evolving graphs and future directions of research in this area.
